Birmingham City Council received 448 resident flood survey responses and investigations were carried out in 41 areas to determine causes and propose actions.

ref.title: May 2018 Flooding: Flood and Water Management Act, Section 19 Investigation

info.text: Widespread flooding of highways, open spaces and properties across Birmingham.

ref.title: May 2018 Flooding: Flood and Water Management Act, Section 19 Investigation

info.text: Widespread flooding across the city following the storm on 27 May 2018: waterlogged gardens, impassable roads, water outflowing from highway gullies, rivers breaching banks, manholes and sewers surcharging and internal property flooding.

ref.title: May 2018 Flooding: Flood and Water Management Act, Section 19 Investigation

info.text: Two distinct zones within the city were affected by flooding on 27 May 2018: a larger south‑west area (including Northfield, Selly Oak and Edgbaston) and a smaller north‑east area (parts of Sutton Coldfield). Flooding followed exceptional, highly localised rainfall (up to 90 mm recorded in the south of the city).

ref.title: May 2018 Flooding: Flood and Water Management Act, Section 19 Investigation

ref.title: May 2018 Flooding: Flood and Water Management Act, Section 19 Investigation

ref.title: May 2018 Flooding: Flood and Water Management Act, Section 19 Investigation

info.text: During the storm on 27 May 2018, runoff from surrounding public open space followed the natural topography toward the rear of properties; existing drainage adjacent to properties was overwhelmed, water levels rose and entered properties from the rear. In the Druids Heath and Monyhull - Sherston Covert area this resulted in internal flooding of properties.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Old Amersham, Amersham January – February 2014

info.text: Town experienced elevated river levels and backing up of the River Misbourne after prolonged above-average rainfall and exceptionally high groundwater levels. ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Old Amersham, Amersham January – February 2014

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Old Amersham, Amersham January – February 2014

info.text: A documented flood event in January–February 2014 affected Old Amersham: high groundwater and raised river levels, plus a culvert blockage caused the River Misbourne to back up, a blocked drainage asset generated a secondary flow down the High Street, and a riverbank collapse caused property flooding. These impacts are described in a Section 19 Flood Investigation report.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Old Amersham, Amersham 15th June 2016

info.text: Properties on the High Street were flooded; at least one property flooded internally during the event described in this report (January–February 2014). ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Old Amersham, Amersham 15th June 2016

info.text: Old Amersham experienced a prolonged period of flooding (Nov 2013 to mid‑Feb 2014) with particularly severe events on 17 Jan 2014 and 06–07 Feb 2014. Saturated catchment and heavy rainfall produced large runoff that, together with high River Misbourne levels, exceeded the capacity of the river and highway drainage. Local drainage assets were flow‑restricted: the culvert under The Maltings was partly restricted; High Street gullies were partly blocked with sediment and largely unable to discharge because of high Misbourne levels; downstream weirs and sedimentation impeded flushing and contributed to backing up of water and reduced culvert outflow. A riverbank collapse on 07 Feb 2014 downstream of the Jaguar garage allowed river water to flow into surrounding areas. Overall the drainage infrastructure could not adequately convey additional surface and highway runoff.

ref.title: Chalfont St Giles, March to April 2014

info.text: The River Misbourne experienced prolonged high water levels from November 2013 to mid-February 2014, with two particularly severe flooding events on/around 17 January and 06/07 February 2014. The high river levels and saturated catchment caused the river and highway drainage to be exceeded, contributed to surface and highway runoff, and a riverbank collapse occurred downstream of the Jaguar garage on 07 February 2014, allowing river water to flow into surrounding areas. Sedimentation and weirs downstream of The Maltings impeded flushing and exacerbated conveyance problems.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Old Amersham, Amersham January – February 2014

info.text: High river levels and a partial flow restriction within a culvert beneath The Maltings caused flooding of gardens and High Street properties in Old Amersham. Removal of an obstruction to a flap valve on 18 January ended the bulk of High Street flooding. A pump was installed on 06 February and jetting of the restricted culvert (11–12 February) reduced water levels substantially (300 mm drop on 11 Feb and a further 300 mm on 12 Feb) and restored most flow through the culvert. Downstream bank collapse near the Jaguar garage required emergency bank restoration and a boom to protect against pollution. Sandbags and FloodSax were distributed to affected properties.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Old Amersham, Amersham January – February 2014

info.text: Culvert flow restriction and obstructions on the River Misbourne caused flooding of Old Amersham High Street; removal of a flap valve obstruction ended the bulk of High Street flooding. A bank collapse downstream of the Jaguar garage required multi‑agency repair and pollution control. A tree removal downstream lowered water levels and culvert jetting substantially reduced water levels and restored flow; EA planned repairs and later multi‑agency meetings addressed culvert/weir removal to reduce future risk.

ref.title: Chalfont St Peter, January – March 2014

info.text: High water levels of the River Misbourne encroached onto adjacent grassy areas and banks; photos show the Misbourne at Church Mead (08/02/14), alongside Barn Meadow (09/01/14) and near the New Rectory (08/02/14) with muddy/raised banks and water reaching normally dry margins.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Old Amersham, Amersham January – February 2014

info.text: The River Misbourne experienced prolonged high water levels from November 2013 to mid-February 2014, with two particularly severe flooding events on/around 17 January and 06/07 February 2014. The high river levels and saturated catchment caused the river and highway drainage to be exceeded, contributed to surface and highway runoff, and a riverbank collapse occurred downstream of the Jaguar garage on 07 February 2014, allowing river water to flow into surrounding areas. Sedimentation and weirs downstream of The Maltings impeded flushing and exacerbated conveyance problems.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Old Amersham, Amersham January – February 2014

info.text: High river levels in the River Misbourne, combined with saturated catchment and large surface runoff, exceeded channel and highway drainage capacity. Riverbank collapse allowed river water to flow into surrounding areas; backing up through drainage gullies contributed to flooding of High Street and nearby properties. A partial culvert restriction reduced conveyance until cleared by the EA.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Old Amersham, Amersham January – February 2014

info.text: Fluvial flooding from the River Misbourne affected Old Amersham (15 June 2016), with recommendations to maintain banks and clear vegetation and debris from the channel; prompted advice to sign up for EA Floodline warnings and for riparian owners to undertake clearance.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Old Amersham, Amersham 15th June 2016

info.text: Culvert flow restriction and obstructions on the River Misbourne caused flooding of Old Amersham High Street; removal of a flap valve obstruction ended the bulk of High Street flooding. A bank collapse downstream of the Jaguar garage required multi‑agency repair and pollution control. A tree removal downstream lowered water levels and culvert jetting substantially reduced water levels and restored flow; EA planned repairs and later multi‑agency meetings addressed culvert/weir removal to reduce future risk.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Old Amersham, Amersham January – February 2014

info.text: The Misbourne catchment experienced high river levels driven by above-average rainfall and exceptionally high groundwater; catchment issues (including culvert restriction at St Peter's Court) led to local water backing up and surface water flooding. The catchment was later included in Thames Water's information-gathering exercise into infiltration and groundwater problems.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Old Amersham, Amersham January – February 2014

info.text: Multiple properties along the High Street experienced flooding in several historical events. In winter 2000/01 basement flooding and flooding to properties was reported; at least one property flooded internally again in winter 2014. Two businesses reported that flood barriers installed after 2000/01 protected their premises in 2014.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Old Amersham, Amersham 15th June 2016

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Old Amersham, Amersham January – February 2014

info.text: High Street gullies designed to discharge to the River Misbourne were partly blocked with sediment and were largely unable to discharge at full capacity because of high water levels in the Misbourne, reducing highway drainage capacity and contributing to surface water/urban flooding of the highway and surrounding area.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Old Amersham, Amersham January – February 2014

info.text: On and after 17 January 2014 the High Street was flooded (road and above kerb line) when a flap valve was blocked, causing river water to back up through a nearby gully and flow eastward along the street; water entered basements (notably the Elephant and Castle pub). Parking and movement of temporary defences affected flow paths. The most severe event overnight 06-07 February 2014 caused internal flooding of properties along the High Street for several days. The primary cause included a partial culvert restriction under The Maltings; EA bypass pumping and culvert jetting (from 12 Feb 2014) removed the restriction and halted further flooding.

ref.title: S19 Flood Investigation Report River Ash and Knowle Green Area

info.text: Complex multi-channel Lower Colne system experienced backwater because high Thames levels prevented normal discharge; tributaries and channels backed up, spilling into the Staines Aqueduct and contributing to the flooding seen in Staines-upon-Thames during the winter 2013/14 event.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Oxford Road New Denham February 2014

info.text: High water levels on the River Colne (linked to high River Thames levels in Feb 2014) meant smaller ditches in the catchment could not drain; as a result water spilled onto adjacent land and onto the highway causing access flooding.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: December 2013-June 2014

info.text: River Colne levels rose quickly and water flowed onto back gardens, causing inundation concerns; residents contacted the Council and sandbags were provided. The Longford Flood Alleviation Scheme (an overflow channel) appeared to function well and likely reduced inundation.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: December 2013-June 2014

info.text: Flows from the River Colne were controlled via an EA-owned sluice gate to manage flood levels in the River Ash; the Environment Agency overrode the sluice gate's automatic settings during the February event to control flooding into Priory Green and surrounding areas.

ref.title: S19 Flood Investigation Report River Ash and Knowle Green Area

info.text: The EA-operated sluice gate controlling flow from the River Colne to the River Ash was manipulated to minimise flood flows from the Colne entering the Ash: closed on 9 February and closed again on 11 February (later reopened on 13 February to restore base flow to the Ash).

ref.title: S19 Flood Investigation Report River Ash and Knowle Green Area

info.text: Very high River Colne levels prevented an ordinary watercourse from discharging. The high river levels contributed to water flowing into a residential garden, onto the highway and into the entrance/internal areas of a College.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: December 2013-June 2014

info.text: The Colne exceeded channel capacity in locations across the winter 2013/14 period, producing notable flooding problems at Watford and Staines; the Colne/Ash catchment response was principally driven by the 6–8 February 2014 storm when antecedent saturation produced very large peak river flows.

ref.title: Section 19 Flood Investigation Report: Spelthorne

info.text: The River (Colne) reached elevated fluvial levels during the event; modelled flood level was approximately 1.278 m (between the 1 in 50-year and 1 in 100-year return periods). High river levels reduced the ability of local surface-water drains to discharge to the river, affecting drainage on Willowbank and adjacent areas; Environment Agency banks and the Willowbank weirs controlled and split flows around Willowbank island during the high flows.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Oxford Road New Denham February 2014

info.text: High flows in the River Colne flowed around King's Island and fed water into the Grand Union Canal, contributing to elevated canal levels and downstream flooding; a sluice next to King's Island main gate was opened (to manage flows).

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Oxford Road New Denham February 2014

info.text: Groundwater across the Colne catchment was reported as 'exceptionally high' during the flooding period, and saturated soils (SMD = 0 in February 2014) meant continued rainfall produced widespread runoff and elevated river levels across the catchment; the EA treated the three-month period leading up to 08 March 2014 as a single event because of groundwater influence.

info.text: A flood incident occurred in Medmenham during the January–February 2014 event, prompting an investigation. The village lies immediately adjacent to the River Thames with the main route (Ferry Lane) running down to the river; the settlement includes low-lying open areas, fields and drainage ditches alongside the Thames that are described in the investigation context as relevant to the flood incident.

ref.title: Medmenham January & February 2014

info.text: The village is on a natural floodplain south of the A4155 and was affected by flooding dominated by the River Thames. Flood Zone 3 / the 1-in-100-year model extent covers almost the entire village; low-lying land (~30–31 m AOD) and properties along Ferry Lane and near New Lock Lane lie within the floodplain and were at risk of inundation. There are no flood defences on this stretch of river, increasing exposure.

ref.title: Medmenham January & February 2014

info.text: The River Thames rose and broke its banks west of Medmenham, sending floodwater north-east across the floodplain into the village. Flooding progressed up Ferry Lane from the slipway, affected the eastern side of Medmenham Abbey and, once banks had breached further west, created a dominant NE flow that inundated wetlands and led to property flooding in the southern half of Ferry Lane (notably south of the white bridge and Abbey Cottages). Some raised properties were surrounded by water.

ref.title: Medmenham January & February 2014

info.text: Flooding from the River Thames overtopping affected the Medmenham area in January–February 2014. Properties were inundated; most residents remained in their homes, some used pumps to limit ingress, and two houses were evacuated. Access to some houses was prevented by deep floodwater on local roads (notably Ferry Lane). A tractor taxi was used to move people because roads were unsafe.

ref.title: Medmenham January & February 2014

info.text: Flooding from the River Thames and backed-up flows inundated gardens, drives and local roads. Gardens and drive were fully immersed to depths reported between 30 cm and 1 m (about 0.5 m average). A house flooded to a maximum depth of 20 cm in February 2014; other houses had no water inside in January 2014. The boat yard area was flooded (estimated inches depth). Water reached up Ferry Lane to Southlands and covered a bridge; water was reported just inside Abbey Gates and at the level of Weybrooks garage. Bucks Fire & Rescue Service recorded 15 properties flooded in Medmenham during the event.

ref.title: Medmenham January & February 2014

info.text: Low-lying areas in Medmenham were flooded when Thames water flowed up Ferry Lane from the south, flooding the road and houses. Ferry Lane and the road were made impassable (only passable by boat or tractor). During the February 2014 episode water was still coming up Ferry Lane (noted 21 Feb) then by 22 Feb was mostly draining via roadside ditches and puddles remained.

ref.title: Thornborough Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: Repeated flooding of the village from ordinary watercourses, surface water and the River Great Ouse across multiple events: 1902 (whole village flooded, several houses flooded by rapid ingress), 1935 (storm — brook at Bridge Street burst its banks, forced down a brick wall, water rose rapidly to around 6 ft and entered houses to ~1 ft depth; many properties affected), March 1947 (overtopping of the River Great Ouse led to ordinary watercourses overtopping and High Street/Back Street and the village green being flooded to about 6 ft), April 1998 (heavy rainfall led to very high river levels and road/ford flooding), July 2000 (internal/external flooding affecting the village), 2006 (two properties reported flooded), July 2007 (around 10 properties flooded; River Great Ouse believed to have flooded the Thornborough Mill area), and the reported event on 23 December 2020 when the village was the subject of the investigation. Impacts described include inundation of streets (High Street, Back Street, The Green), internal property flooding, damage to carpets and furniture, and significant depths of standing water in parts of the village and at the ford on Back Street.

Fly‑tipped debris in the highway ditch beside the IDB‑maintained watercourse was identified as obstructing flow and a potential contributor to flooding. A section of watercourse flows to a pumping station alongside Lower Road.

ref.title: Thornborough Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

ref.title: Thornborough Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

ref.title: Thornborough Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: On 23 December 2020 the village experienced intense surface water and river-related flooding. At least five residential properties suffered internal flooding. Multiple ordinary watercourses and culverts were overtopped in the village, roads became unpassable, drains were blocked and overwhelmed, and a manhole cover lifted with flood water near properties. Water backed up from sewers into toilets (reported on Bridge Street). Concentrated overland flows and runoff from saturated surrounding fields contributed to flooding across streets. At the junction of Back Street and Lower End at least 13 cars became stranded and flooded requiring Fire Brigade attendance. Residents leaving the village hall had to wade through significant flooding on the High Street during an episode starting between 19:00–20:00 and lasting roughly five hours, causing major disruption and distress.

ref.title: Gawcott Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: The village experienced flooding of the highway (Main Street) during the 23rd December 2020 event — including a surcharged manhole and surface water inundation. Flooding was associated with upstream open ordinary watercourses conveyed through two upstream culverts and a main culvert under Main Street, plus highway gullies which were found to drain into the culverted watercourses (not the public combined sewer). Private property surface water discharges into either the combined sewer or the surface water culvert, which likely contributed to capacity exceedance and surcharging.

ref.title: Gawcott Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: During the 23rd December 2020 event, Main Street in Gawcott was flooded and a manhole in Main Street was observed surcharged. Highway gullies within the village drain into culverted watercourses (not the combined sewer) according to the commissioned survey; CCTV and survey work identified defects in the culverted watercourse (e.g. holes in culvert wall, masonry in the base producing ~40% blockage, reductions in culvert diameter) which contributed to flow restriction and local flooding of the street.

ref.title: Gawcott Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: The Gawcott catchment experienced intense, two-wave rainfall on 23 December 2020 that fell on already wet soils with minimal additional storage capacity, producing rapid runoff across the catchment and causing flooding within the Gawcott area. The storm passed across the catchment in a northerly then southerly direction during the event.

ref.title: Gawcott Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: The 23 December 2020 storm produced rapid runoff on an already saturated catchment leading to flooding; a hydraulic model was used to represent flood levels and extents on the ordinary watercourse. The modelling estimates an approximate flow return period of 50–75 years and indicates a peak flow of about 0.9 m3/s. The rainfall event itself had a ~14% annual exceedance probability (≈7-year return) but the saturated soils made the catchment very sensitive and quick to respond, contributing to the flood impacts modelled at Gawcott.

Residents reported significant distress, insurance claims and financial impacts.

ref.title: Gawcott Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: The culverted watercourse running through Gawcott was surveyed and found to have blockages, intrusions and structural defects (including holes) reducing capacity and leaving sections at risk of collapse; these culvert conditions are associated with flooding of local property (for example the Methodist Chapel).

ref.title: Gawcott Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: The village culverted watercourse along Main Street has frequent and severe defects and blockages that reduced culvert capacity and contributed to surcharging, manhole exceedance and flooding in the village during the 23rd December 2020 event. CCTV and survey evidence show partial blockages (masonry, rubble, roots and pipe intrusions), pipe size reductions and structural holes that risk collapse and caused the survey to be abandoned in places. A 300mm foul misconnection was identified between SW02 and SW01 and is likely the source of foul debris observed downstream. The defects therefore increased the likelihood and severity of surface water flooding and led to sewer/foul contamination impacts to downstream properties/areas; urgent repairs and maintenance were recommended to avoid collapse, backing up or future flooding.

info.text: Surface water flooding affected the village on 23 December 2020. The culverted watercourse and surface water drainage were overloaded and the hydraulic model was verified to replicate the flood depths experienced that day.

ref.title: Gawcott Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

The investigation modelled mitigation options for Gawcott including increasing culvert capacity, adding gullies on Main Street, and upstream storage areas to reduce runoff towards Main Street.

ref.title: Gawcott Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

The culvert capacity limitations contributed to flood depths; even if the culvert had been clear and in good condition the village would still have flooded in that event, although depths would have been reduced by culvert improvements.

ref.title: Gawcott Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

ref.title: Gawcott Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: Main Street experienced overtopping/surface water inundation during the event; a manhole was observed surcharged and photos show flooding of the carriageway. The surcharging and surface flooding were linked to constrained culverted flows and defects in the surface water culvert (hole in culvert wall, masonry in base, pipe crossings, reductions in culvert diameter and blockages) which reduced conveyance and led to highway flooding.

ref.title: Gawcott Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: Floodwater flowed down both streets (Main Street and New Inn Lane), pooling at a low spot and causing internal property flooding.

ref.title: Gawcott Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: Road closures were put in place and sandbags were delivered to the street; access and transport were disrupted and residents on the street required assistance to dispose of flood-damaged furnishings (skip arranged by the parish council).

ref.title: Gawcott Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: Traffic driving through floodwater on Main Street washed water into properties located on Main Street; culvert surcharge and manhole lifting occurred along the culvert beneath Main Street during the 23 December 2020 event.

ref.title: Gawcott Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: Highway flooding was significant along these roads (Main Street and New Inn Lane), prompting transport disruption and contributing to a road closure.

ref.title: Gawcott Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: Highway flooding inundated the full carriageway and encroached onto adjacent properties and driveways, impeding vehicle and pedestrian movement. Buckinghamshire Council (the Highway Authority) ordered a road closure after 18:00 on 23rd December 2020.

ref.title: Gawcott Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: The culverted watercourse running along Main Street was found to have blockages, intrusions and pipe size changes that reduced capacity; short sections were impassable. A Grade 5 defect (a hole) was identified close to the Methodist Chapel between manholes SW01 and SW02, with another similar hole observed on CCTV.

ref.title: Gawcott Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: Survey identified a 300mm foul misconnection between inspection points SW02 and SW01 discharging into the 600mm brick sewer beneath the street; foul debris from this connection has been observed by residents downstream, indicating contamination of surface waters and water-quality impacts associated with the flood event.

ref.title: Gawcott Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: The main culverted watercourse running the length of Main Street was overloaded during the event on 23 December 2020, causing surface water flooding on/around Main Street; culvert blockages and poor condition contributed to the flooding.

ref.title: Gawcott Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: Conveyance under Main Street was a key failure point: the culvert beneath Main Street is in very poor condition with blockages, pipe-size constrictions, sedimentation and rough material that reduced conveyance causing surcharge and flooding onto Main Street (a manhole on Main Street was observed surcharged during the event). Modelling tested removing blockages and smoothing the culvert and also tested increasing culvert capacity and additional gullies to reduce surface water flooding.

ref.title: Gawcott Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: The culvert under Main Street was blocked/defective and its capacity was exceeded during the 23 December 2020 event, causing flooding along Main Street (surcharging and local ponding). Modelling indicates relining would not have prevented flooding on 23 Dec 2020 (though it would have reduced recession times and reduced impacts in lower‑order events); enlarging or adding a parallel culvert could have prevented flooding caused by culvert capacity being exceeded, though ponding from rainfall may still have occurred.

ref.title: Gawcott Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: Constrained sections of the Main Street culvert (most of the culvert is 600mm but with short 300mm and 150mm sections and other constrictions) reduced conveyance. During the 23 December 2020 event these restrictions contributed to flooding on Main Street and slowed recession of flood levels. Blockages of masonry and roots were present in problematic sections; targeted clearing/relining and repairs are being proposed to stabilise damaged sections and remove blockages, which would reduce impacts and speed recession though would likely not have prevented flooding on 23 December 2020.

ref.title: Gawcott Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: The culvert beneath Main Street is identified as a critical infrastructure element whose capacity was predicted to be exceeded in the 1-in-10 annual chance event; exceedance of this culvert contributed to flooding at and around Main Street. The condition of the culvert is noted as an unresolved issue increasing flood risk.

info.text: The Main Street culvert was subject to excessive pressure from surface water runoff during the December 2020 flood; restricted culvert capacity and downstream channel/pond condition were cited as factors that increased flood impacts in the village.

ref.title: Tingewick Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: During the 23 December 2020 event properties in Tingewick experienced internal flooding with numerous reports of water rising through floors. Groundwater was identified as being shallow in large areas of the village (within 0.025–0.5 m and 0.5–5 m of the surface in places) and likely contributed to flooding alongside surface water from local watercourses and pond overtopping.

ref.title: Tingewick Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: Tingewick experienced repeated surface-water flooding events over time, resulting in internal flooding to multiple properties (April 1998, July 2007, 2014). The investigation documents flooding associated with the 23 December 2020 event in the village (including documented pond flooding/overtopping on 23 December 2020).

ref.title: Tingewick Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: The village was flooded on 23 December 2020; the event prompted the establishment of the Tingewick Flood Response Team and purchase of response equipment (pumps, hoses, dehumidifiers and sandbags) funded by a Buckinghamshire Council grant to support future responses.

ref.title: Tingewick Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: On 23 December 2020 intense rainfall over a saturated catchment produced a rapid catchment response; radar and gauge data show substantial rainfall (radar total ~48 mm; local gauge record nearby up to 52 mm) falling on soils with very low moisture deficit (0–10 mm), which led to rapid runoff and surface-water/flash flooding across the Tingewick catchment.

ref.title: Tingewick Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: Flooding in the village on 23 December 2020 from heavy rainfall and rapid catchment response on already-saturated soils. Residents were affected and received assistance from Buckinghamshire Fire and Rescue Service and Transport for Buckinghamshire. A hydraulic model was used to recreate flood levels and extents; modelled flows implied an approximate return period of over 50 years.

ref.title: Tingewick Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: Flood water emerged through manholes and flooded the highway and gardens; internal property flooding occurred (water rising through floors) affecting multiple properties; roads were closed during the event and remaining flood water receded overnight into 24 December.

ref.title: Tingewick Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: Identified as a significant area of flooding; roads flooded and communities were cut off; local residents used pumps and sandbags to try to protect properties; the Parish Council formed a Tingewick Emergency Response Team and supplied sandbags, pumps and manhole keys for future events; a house fire occurred in Tingewick caused by electrical damage to a boiler directly resulting from the flooding.

ref.title: Tingewick Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: Intense rainfall on an already saturated catchment caused the ordinary watercourse to rise rapidly and widespread overland flow through the village. A culvert running under Main Street was surcharged and its capacity exceeded, several manholes along Main Street surcharged, blocked gullies and a collapsed surface water pipe (below West Well Lane) exacerbated flow. Surface water followed Main Street and West Well Lane, leading to internal property flooding (including properties adjacent to the Education Facility).

ref.title: Tingewick Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: Overtopping of Townsend Pond led to floodwater flowing down Main Street and extensive internal and external flooding across the village. At least 20 properties were flooded internally (including one commercial property, The Royal Oak, and 19 residential properties). Many residents were forced into temporary accommodation, reported insurance claims and financial burden, and experienced mental-health impacts and stress. Internal flooding entered properties through front doors and in some cases through floors; floodwater depths were worst towards the western end of Main Street. Flooding began after pond overtopping around 17:00 and dissipated rapidly from about 23:00, with no remaining flooding after 02:00 on 24 December as the pond level fell and the culverted watercourse drained the road.

ref.title: Tingewick Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: Internal and external flooding across the village: extensive internal flooding of properties (including whole-ground-floor inundation in worst cases), prolonged drying times for homes, damage to carpets/flooring/furniture, one property’s boiler damaged by flooding which subsequently caused a house fire. At least some households were displaced or lived on upper floors while repairs occurred.

ref.title: Tingewick Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: The culverted watercourse through Tingewick (along Main Street) and connecting surface water sewer were obstructed during the observed flood event, which slowed discharge to the downstream open watercourse. A 35% vegetation blockage was identified at the downstream end of the culvert and the downstream connection from the West Well Lane surface water sewer into the culvert was partially blocked by masonry bricks and root growth; these conditions were reproduced in the hydraulic baseline model for the 23 December 2020 flood.

ref.title: Tingewick Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: Surface water flooding affected the village on 23 December 2020; the surface water drainage system was overloaded (model baseline calibrated to reported flood depths for that date). A collapsed culvert on West Well Lane prior to the event caused backing up of water that contributed to the flooding.

ref.title: Tingewick Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: Flooding from the ordinary watercourse affected the village; modelling of the 23 December 2020 event considered an upstream storage area to the west of the village which, in the model, operates online and captures water from the ordinary watercourse as a mitigation measure.

ref.title: Tingewick Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: The surface water/ordinary watercourse culvert through the village was at capacity and surcharged during the 23rd December 2020 event, causing flooding in the village. Modelled results indicate the culvert was overloaded above a 1 in 10 annual chance event and surcharging occurred; very large upstream storage (estimated 15,000–20,000 m3 for the December 2020 event, ~6,000 m3 for a 1% AEP design event) would have been required to reduce flows.

ref.title: Tingewick Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: The ordinary watercourse culvert upstream of the village was overloaded in the 23 December 2020 event, producing flood flows into the village. Floodwater entered many properties through doors and floors; a number of affected properties had suspended timber floors and low-level airbricks which contributed to internal entry.

ref.title: Tingewick Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: During the December 2020 event water entered many properties in Tingewick via multiple points, including doors and through floors; many affected properties had suspended timber floors and ground‑level airbricks which contributed to internal ingress and property flooding.

ref.title: Tingewick Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: The village experienced flooding on 23 December 2020; the severity was noted to be increased by blockage of highway gullies leading to surface water accumulation and added pressure on the village surface water culvert and receiving watercourse. Balancing ponds associated with the Tingewick Bypass were reviewed and concluded not to have been a significant factor in the village flooding (eastern pond discharges downstream of the village; the western pond was designed with capacity and an outfall limiting discharge).

ref.title: Tingewick Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: The village experienced rapid flooding on 23 December 2020. The ordinary watercourse rose rapidly and a 600mm culvert beneath Main Street was surcharged, while private drainage connections and manholes surcharged causing water to flood out into rear gardens and back up into properties. At least 20 properties flooded internally (including residential and one commercial property) and a further two properties experienced external or outbuilding flooding. Internal flooding entered mainly via rear doors; many ground-floor rooms flooded and six properties reported the entire ground floor flooded. One property suffered a fire due to a boiler damaged by floodwater.

ref.title: Tingewick Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: Internal flooding affected properties in the village: at least 20 properties flooded internally (including one commercial property, The Royal Oak). Internal flooding was extensive—at least six properties reported flooding to the entire ground floor and the remainder had flooding to individual rooms on the ground floor. Internal flood depths were typically 75–200 mm (a small number 300–600 mm). External flood depths were typically 150–600 mm. One property suffered a boiler-related fire caused by flood damage. Highway flooding was significant and mental-health impacts and community concern about future flooding were reported.

ref.title: Tingewick Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

info.text: During a site visit in May 2021 several gullies in the village were found to be blocked, preventing drainage from the highway at those locations. Previous reports of flooding also note gullies in the village become blocked, contributing to local surface water/urban flooding and impaired highway drainage.

info.text: The rainfall-accumulation radar for 20 September 2014 shows very high, localized rainfall over Chesham and its immediate west/southwest surroundings. ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Chesham 20 September 2014

info.text: On 20 September 2014 intense rainfall caused surface water runoff and increased flows in the River Chess and its tributary the Vale Brook. In parts of the town these increased flows exceeded the capacity of infrastructure (notably the Vale Brook culvert), resulting in flooding of parts of Chesham.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Chesham 20 September 2014

info.text: Multiple areas within the town experienced property flooding during the incident (areas A, B and C are highlighted as locations where residential and business properties flooded).

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Chesham 20 September 2014

info.text: Town centre was affected by flooding driven by the Vale Brook receiving surface water from much of Chesham's urban area and limited channel capacity; flood and surface-water risk prompted mapping of fluvial and surface water flood extents in the town centre.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Chesham 20 September 2014

info.text: A very localised, intense overnight storm (19–20 Sept 2014) produced heavy rainfall over the town; radar shows highest accumulation over Chesham (particularly High Street and Pednormead End neighbourhoods). The intense rainfall caused rapid rises in local watercourses (see Vale Brook) and contributed to acute urban/flash flooding conditions in the town. Water levels rose and fell quickly in response to the storm.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Chesham 20 September 2014

info.text: At least 34 properties were internally flooded (5 residential, 29 businesses). Surface-water ponding in Market Square and along the High Street exceeded slot drains causing overland flows (southern High Street flowed overland for about an hour); most shop flooding penetrated only a few metres to depths of about 2–5 cm. Vale Brook culvert manholes within at least three High Street/Broadway shops surcharged. Market Square section of the Vale Brook culvert experienced sand compaction from the event, causing collapse of brick pavers at the surface (surface damage) though the culvert performance was not affected.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Chesham 20 September 2014

info.text: An intense, highly localised rainfall event (approx. 03:00–05:00) produced widespread surface water flooding across Chesham. Up to around Pednormead End and the town centre the event led to overwhelmed drainage, backed-up culverts/manholes, and surface water entering properties; property owners cleaned floors, removed damaged carpet tiles and used dehumidifiers. Surface water had largely drained away by about 06:00, and no immediate multi-agency incident response occurred because agencies were unaware until the following Monday.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Chesham 20 September 2014

info.text: The town experienced flooding on 20 September 2014; a number of issues contributed to the event (including problems associated with the Vale Brook culvert).

info.text: The town experienced flooding associated with the investigated event (20 September 2014). ref.title: Tingewick Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

ref.title: Tingewick Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

ref.title: Ley Hill Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

ref.title: Ley Hill Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

ref.title: Ley Hill Section 19 Flood Investigation: Final Technical Report

ref.title: Barnet Section 19 Flood Investigation

info.text: On 12 July 2021 heavy rainfall caused widespread flooding across the London Borough of Barnet. The borough received 40 reports of flooding (17 internal, 4 external and 19 highway). The evidence indicates the sewer network became overwhelmed due to lack of capacity and high surface-water runoff, causing internal, external and highway flooding. High water levels in the Mutton Brook reduced discharge from surface water sewers and further impacted sewer capacity.

ref.title: Bolton Council Flooding Investigation Report: Flooding at Horwich and Lostock on 16th May 2021

info.text: On 16th May 2021 very intense rainfall produced rapid runoff from undeveloped land to the north‑west of Horwich that overwhelmed existing drainage capacity. United Utilities attended properties that reported flooding in the days following the event and carried out CCTV inspections, finding no significant operational blockages that could have caused or contributed to the flooding.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Greater Manchester 26 December 2015

info.text: Widespread river and surface-water flooding across the Irwell, Roch and Croal catchments: 37 of 44 river-level gauges recorded their highest-ever levels. Flooding exceeded defence levels used for infrastructure resilience. Large-scale electricity supply loss across the conurbation (see local breakdowns); six electrical sub-stations were flooded or damaged, mobile generators were mobilised. Multiple bridges were damaged or displaced; some required extensive permanent repairs.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Greater Manchester 26 December 2015

info.text: Widespread flooding across the region caused transport disruption (tram services suspended on several routes; major rail services disrupted and route checks required; road closures, diversions and impassable roads), damage to Environment Agency assets and river defences (including destruction/damage of river gauging stations), and flooding at wastewater treatment works and pumping stations which affected treatment processes and recovery operations. Local authority offices in town centres were flooded, affecting servers and slowing recovery coordination.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Greater Manchester 26 December 2015

info.text: Widespread flood impacts across the county included inundation and operational disruption of wastewater treatment works (Bury flooded; Rochdale and Urmston affected), combined sewer overflow discharges and polluted runoff affecting water quality, mobilisation and deposition of large quantities of gravel and masonry rubble altering channels and increasing local flood or erosion risk, habitat damage and potential spread of invasive species, and local slope failures beside watercourses due to waterlogged ground.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Greater Manchester 26 December 2015

info.text: A major incident was declared and a multi‑agency response operated across the area. Rest centres were opened for displaced people. Significant repair works were required to highways, cycle paths, footpaths, river channels, retaining walls and drainage systems. An extensive cleanup operation collected and disposed of waste and debris. Electricity substations were inundated and defences overtopped causing power losses; Distribution Network Operators undertook emergency repairs. United Utilities saw a large increase in wastewater incidents and attended many sites; properties were flooded from sewers. A Recovery Coordinating Group was formed to manage recovery activity.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Greater Manchester 26 December 2015

info.text: The EA surface water flood map for Billinge shows areas of low-to-high surface water flood risk concentrated in low-lying areas and along watercourses; residential streets (including Brownheath Avenue and Powell Drive) and some community assets lie near or within risk zones. Once MFRS cleared the culverts the watercourse stopped overtopping and highway drainage was able to clear floodwater.

ref.title: Section 19 Investigation Report: June 2016 Flood Events

ref.title: Section 19 Investigation Report: June 2016 Flood Events

info.text: Widespread property flooding across the borough during June 2016. Short-duration, high-intensity rainfall events on 8, 10 and 16 June caused surface water / flash flooding, while a longer-duration event on 11 June produced raised river levels (notably Poise Brook) causing fluvial flooding in parts of the borough (for example Hazel Grove and Offerton Green).

ref.title: Section 19 Investigation Report: June 2016 Flood Events

info.text: Multiple communities across the borough experienced property flooding. On 8 June 2016 there were 75 properties flooded (all recorded as sewer flooding). On 10 June 2016 there were 30 properties flooded (predominantly sewer flooding with some incidents caused by groundwater). Additional significant property flooding occurred in parts of the borough on 11 June 2016.

ref.title: Section 19 Investigation Report: June 2016 Flood Events

info.text: Parts of the Stockport borough (notably the Offerton Green suburb) experienced repeated residential property flooding during the June 2016 extreme rainfall events, including internal flooding and evacuations.

ref.title: Section 19 Investigation Report: June 2016 Flood Events

info.text: The Offerton Green suburb of Stockport suffered multiple flood events in June 2016: intense rainfall on 8 June overwhelmed surface water sewers causing external and internal property flooding; repeated flooding occurred on 11 June from surface water and later river (Poise Brook) flooding; lower-severity rainfall on 16 June caused repeat flooding at Holiday Lane. Flooding led to property inundation, internal flooding, resident evacuations and local road closures.

ref.title: Section 19 Investigation Report: June 2016 Flood Events

info.text: Parts of the Stockport borough were affected by property flooding in June 2016, notably Cheadle where sewer blockages and surface water ponding caused repeated internal and commercial property flooding.

ref.title: Section 19 Investigation Report: June 2016 Flood Events

info.text: June 2016 flooding damaged highway infrastructure and greenspace across the borough. Bramhall Happy Valley Park had footpaths damaged or swept away; public rights of way lost footpaths and footbridges; the Council has been undertaking repairs and identifying funding for remaining works.

ref.title: Section 19 Investigation Report: June 2016 Flood Events

info.text: Widespread flooding across the borough during June 2016 that affected multiple communities and prompted the borough-wide investigation and recommended actions (e.g. maintain highway drains, review flood management and alert trigger levels).

ref.title: Section 19 Flood Investigation Report for July 2019 Event

info.text: The Metropolitan Borough of Stockport was heavily impacted by the storms (28–31 July 2019) with widespread flooding and transport disruption; large numbers of internal and external property flood reports were raised; surface water flooding occurred at many locations and some watercourses had very high flows causing bank flooding and overtopping at bridges and culverts.

ref.title: Section 19 Flood Investigation Report for July 2019 Event

info.text: The borough experienced widespread flooding that prompted the Section 19 investigation; the report reviews causes and major impacts across the most affected areas ('hotspots') and considers previous 2016 flood events.

ref.title: Section 19 Flood Investigation Report for July 2019 Event

info.text: The July 2019 flood event caused flooding across the borough; the extent of that flooding renewed concerns that the A555 Manchester Airport Relief Road’s construction and subsequent water-management performance may have worsened flood risk to watercourses (Poynton Brook, Lady Brook, Micker Brook) and adjacent communities.

ref.title: Section 19 Flood Investigation Report for July 2019 Event

info.text: The report states that the incidence of flooding was widespread across the borough during the 2019 events, with many isolated incidents and identified local flooding 'hot spots' that were reviewed as part of the investigation.

ref.title: Section 19 Flood Investigation Report for July 2019 Event

info.text: Widespread flooding across the borough during 28 Jul 2019 - 31 Jul 2019, with many isolated incidents and locally concentrated 'hot spots'. Critical catchments implicated include Micker/Lady/Poynton/Norbury Brooks and Poise Brook, where runoff conveyed from large upstream areas caused localised inundation of communities and infrastructure; hot-spot locations were reviewed in appendices C–N.

ref.title: Section 19 Flood Investigation Report for July 2019 Event

info.text: Severe rainfall across the borough between 28 and 31 July 2019 exceeded surface water drainage design standards over a large area, so widespread surface water flooding was expected and flooding on ordinary watercourses was likely; reduced available storage (e.g. attenuation ponds on the A555 still draining) further increased runoff and flood risk.

ref.title: Section 19 Flood Investigation Report for July 2019 Event

info.text: Multiple ordinary watercourses within the Stockport area were the subject of clear-up operations and flood warnings/alerts during the July 2019 events; local RMAs investigated reported incidences of flooding across the borough.

ref.title: Section 19 Flood Investigation Report for July 2019 Event

info.text: The borough experienced widespread flooding in July 2019 with a significantly greater incidence compared to earlier events; local flood incident logging systems (LLFA) were overwhelmed, and RMA response was largely reactive. This prompted recognition of the need for improved asset registers and stronger proactive maintenance/checking of critical structures.

ref.title: Section 19 Flood Investigation Report for July 2019 Event

info.text: Multiple locations within Stockport experienced flooding issues during the July 2019 event; records of affected areas have been maintained by the investigators.

ref.title: Section 19 Flood Investigation Report for July 2019 Event

info.text: Widespread flooding across the borough with numerous reports and local 'risk to life' incidents (deep/fast flowing waters and inundation threats). Specific locations reported included Bramhall Green, Queens Road, The Demmings, Twinning Brook Road (fast/deep flows) and basement flooding at Guywood Lane, Romiley; additional inundation threat reports (9) related to the Toddbrook Reservoir incident affecting the Strines/Whaley Bridge area.

ref.title: Section 19 Flood Investigation Report for July 2019 Event

info.text: Widespread flooding across the borough during late July 2019 with multiple sources: surface water/overland flows, highway flooding, watercourse blockages and capacities of watercourses/sewers/drains being exceeded. 776 flood reports were received by RMAs (majority on 31 July 2019). Peak flows were recorded on the River Goyt and Poynton Brook on 31 July; 'risk to life' conditions were reported at Bramhall Green, Queens Road, The Demmings and Twinning Brook Road due to deep, fast-flowing Lady/Micker Brook waters and at Guywood Lane, Romiley due to a flooded basement flat. Sandringham Road and The Demmings Industrial Estate experienced flooding beyond the mapped 1,000-year extent. Poise Brook at Offerton Green outflanked a third-party defence along Bean Leach Road and spilled towards a housing estate.

ref.title: Section 19 Flood Investigation Report for July 2019 Event

info.text: Widespread and diverse flooding across the borough during the July 2019 event triggered borough-wide recommendations and local actions; multiple local areas and watercourses experienced flooding and drainage failures requiring targeted investigations and interventions.

ref.title: Section 19 Flood Investigation Report for July 2019 Event

info.text: Flooding incidents affected the A555 within the borough; the road and its drainage had suffered repeated flooding up to July 2019 and the road drainage has the potential to alter runoff to adjacent watercourses in the borough.

ref.title: Section 19 Flood Investigation Report for July 2019 Event

ref.title: Boxing Day Flooding – Greater Manchester section 19 FWMA 2010 investigation report and complementary Salford report

info.text: High water levels in the Manchester Ship Canal prevented surface water drains from discharging, which is likely to have caused carriageway flooding on Cadishead Way in Irlam. Canal-related high water also contributed to elevated water levels at Salford Quays during the event, coincident with loss of pontoons at Agecroft Rowing Club.

ref.title: Boxing Day Flooding – Greater Manchester section 19 FWMA 2010 investigation report and complementary Salford report

info.text: Flooding from the Manchester Ship Canal occurred, with high water levels and flows passing downstream that caused flooding in the vicinity of Irlam and Latchford locks and an area north of Lymm (Thelwall). Erosion of the canal bank occurred immediately downstream of Mode Wheel locks (Salford Quays) and on the Trafford bank of the Ship Canal adjacent to the Valero Energy oil storage facility; the site operator emptied tanks closest to the canal as a precaution against undermining.

ref.title: Boxing Day Flooding – Greater Manchester section 19 FWMA 2010 investigation report and complementary Salford report

info.text: Bank erosion occurred on the canal during the event adjacent to the Valero Energy oil storage facility and on the Trafford bank; canal flow management and related coordination took place during the incident. Modelling noted upstream flooding at nearby locations was independent of canal levels.

ref.title: Boxing Day Flooding – Greater Manchester section 19 FWMA 2010 investigation report and complementary Salford report

info.text: During the flooding the canal bank was eroded adjacent to a COMAH facility downstream of Mode Wheel locks in Salford; the site operator emptied oil tanks closest to the canal as a precaution against potential environmental release if undermined. Hydraulic modelling indicated upstream flood levels at nearby flooded locations were independent of canal levels.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Greater Manchester 26 December 2015

info.text: Flooding associated with the Manchester Ship Canal affected communities, businesses and residences and prompted actions to develop flood-warning provision, improve incident response arrangements and share real-time data between organisations.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Greater Manchester 26 December 2015

info.text: Overtopping of raised defences and natural banks caused widespread flooding of nearby properties and damage to infrastructure. Contributed to flooding of Greenvale Business Park via overtopping and interaction with the flood relief channel. Infrastructure damage linked to the event included culvert damage at Calderbrook Road, Todmorden Road and Halifax Road, and gully blockage and damage to paths.

info.text: The River Roch at Littleborough reached record high levels during the event; high river flows caused surface water to pond against a defence wall (which subsequently collapsed) and prevented surface water from draining away, contributing to flooding in the area. A flood warning was issued for the River Roch at Littleborough.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Greater Manchester 26 December 2015

info.text: Flows in the River Roch through Roch town centre exceeded the capacity of a culvert next to the new bus station, causing river water to flood the town centre. Floodwater travelled along Smith Street and South Parade and re-entered the river downstream; businesses on Smith Street, South Parade, The Butts and The Walk were flooded; Number One Riverside council office was flooded (ground-floor library remained closed after reopening); the town centre bus station and tram terminus sustained flood damage; power loss affected many homes and businesses; the town hall narrowly avoided flooding. Downstream, the Asda superstore, adjacent Curry's PC World and the Sixth Form College suffered internal flood damage and St Mary’s Gate subway was damaged.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Greater Manchester 26 December 2015

info.text: High river flows on the River Roch caused flooding in Rochdale; a formal flood warning area was active and the river gauge at Albert recorded the highest level in 22 years.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Greater Manchester 26 December 2015

info.text: River Roch was the main river source for flooding in the area: properties close to the River Roch were flooded internally (to depths up to 400 mm) and a large portion of the reported flooded properties (35 of 36) were attributed to the main river (River Roch and Hey/Buckley Brook). Cellars adjacent to the River Roch flooded from surface water/groundwater when the brook reached high levels.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Greater Manchester 26 December 2015

info.text: Very high river levels on 26 December 2015 (the gauge at Albert Royds Street recorded its highest level in 22 years) caused flooding of properties adjacent to the River Roch (internal flooding reported, cellars flooded from groundwater/surface water) and contributed to wider flood extent in Rochdale/Wardleworth. Local interventions (assessments, gravel removal and proposals to reduce risk) were initiated after the event.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Greater Manchester 26 December 2015

info.text: Flooding from the River Roch (and its drains) caused rear yard drains of residential properties to fill and then river water entered properties. Flow was gradual at first then became fast; muddy, polluted water flowed into properties to depths of about 600 to 900 mm. info.text: High astronomical spring tides combined with a storm surge on 11-12 March 2020 caused tidal flooding across the Bristol region; roads along the River Avon were significantly impacted and one property flooded internally; no essential infrastructure reported flooded.

ref.title: Flood Investigation: March 2020 Tidal Flooding

info.text: Areas of the city adjacent to the River Avon experienced tidal flooding during the high tides of 11–12 March 2020, with multiple streets, basins and a footpath inundated along the river corridor.

ref.title: Flood Investigation: March 2020 Tidal Flooding

info.text: Central Bristol was affected by a tidal flood event; flood alerts and warnings were issued and the Environment Agency operated sluices and closed flood gates (e.g. Eastville sluice gates to allow River Frome flows to discharge to the River Avon downstream of Black Rocks, and gates at Shirehampton) with pre/post-tide checks and clearances to manage tide locking.

ref.title: Flood Investigation: March 2020 Tidal Flooding

info.text: On 11 March 2020 (and into 12 March 2020) Bristol experienced tidal/coastal flooding caused by an astronomical high tide combined with a storm surge and westerly winds; the event reached a peak of 8.81mAOD and affected several areas across the city, including the Portway and Cattle Market Road.

info.text: Surface water drainage systems in Godmanchester were unable to convey runoff, causing excess surface water to flow over the ground following local topography and putting properties at risk of surface water flooding. ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Offord Cluny & Offord D’arcy

info.text: Widespread flooding across the settlement with internal and external property flooding in multiple areas. Three key risk areas with internal property flooding were identified (High Street North; Station Lane; Parkway/Elm Close/Latin Close/New Road/High Street South). Ingress into properties did not recede for a number of days; some properties lost foul sewerage provision for about three weeks. Significant and prolonged flooding occurred along the B1043 High Street to the north, causing a full road closure. At least eight properties were rendered uninhabitable for between one and eight months.

Flood depths reached approximately 45 cm; highway was closed for approximately 3 weeks; Anglian Water sewer system was impacted leaving some residents without foul sewerage for about 3 weeks. Ingress into properties did not recede for days and at least some properties were made uninhabitable for extended periods (see combined figures).

info.text: The February 2020 storm caused widespread flooding across Calderdale towns (Hebden Bridge, Todmorden, Mytholmroyd, Elland, Sowerby Bridge, Luddenden) producing mass property and infrastructure damage: major roads and bridges were seriously damaged; a significant number of residential and business properties were flooded; eight schools were temporarily closed (two schools experienced significant damage); council buildings including Hebden Bridge library suffered damage.

ref.title: Section 19 Report: Flood Event 9th February 2020

info.text: Across the Calder catchment within Calderdale, river stage hydrographs for the 9 February 2020 event show river levels rising from the early hours and reaching peaks around midday; tributary peaks occurred between about 11:30 and 13:15, indicating a rapid response of 0.5–2.25 hours. ref.title: Section 19 Report: Flood Event 9th February 2020

info.text: Widespread flooding across the borough affecting communities, properties and infrastructure. In Hebden Bridge torrential hillside runoff and surface water flows, combined with River Calder and canal overtopping, caused internal flooding to properties, carriage of large debris and rocks, severe damage where water depths on Oxford Road and Cambridge Street exceeded 1.5 m, damaged bridleways blocking access to Greenland Road and Blackshaw Head, and impacts to structures such as Calis Bridge from high river flows.

ref.title: Section 19 Report: Flood Event 9th February 2020

info.text: Extensive flooding in Hebden Bridge driven by hillside runoff and overtopping of the canal and River Calder. Torrential surface flows channelled down multiple roads (Keighley Road, Birchcliffe, Palace House Road, Mytholm Steeps, Saville Road) causing internal flooding of properties on Keighley Road, Birchcliffe, Hanging Road, Market Street, Oxford Street and Cambridge Street. Properties on Oxford Road and Cambridge Street experienced water depths in excess of 1.5 m, causing severe damage. Debris and large rocks were carried by flows, damaging buildings and infrastructure; bridleway paths were damaged blocking access to Greenland Road and Blackshaw Head. Calis Bridge and Jumble Hole Clough were affected by high river volumes. Large-scale deposition of gravel and sand in the River Calder caused the river to change course, prompting concerns over the stability of the Hebden Bridge Aqueduct. In South Todmorden (Shade Chapel) the culvert carrying Walsden Water beneath the building partially collapsed, damaging the base and sides of the culvert, restricting the channel and threatening blockage; the partial collapse also put the building at risk of falling into the river, which would have increased flood risk to nearby properties.

ref.title: Section 19 Report: Flood Event 9th February 2020

info.text: Significant flooding occurred on 9th February 2020 despite temporary Mytholmroyd FAS measures under construction. Temporary flood barriers and bulk bags were overtopped or undermined by flow (material washed from beneath road edges allowing flow under barriers). Canal towpaths and boundary walls were undercut and cracked; embankments were voided and the canal channel was silted. Temporary defences failed or were overtopped at multiple locations, leading to widespread road and property inundation, garden flooding, cellar flooding and damage to towpath infrastructure.

Numerous soakaways along Caterham Drive were identified and several local soakaways were inspected (site visit 05/08/2016; condition assessments by Flowline in Appendix B); soakaway condition (siltation/blocking) affects the ability to drain runoff and is relevant to the flooding experienced on Caterham Drive.

ref.title: Caterham Drive Flood Investigation Report – 7th June 2016

info.text: On 7 June 2016 the surface water drainage and soakaway network failed to drain the intense rainfall, causing rapid onset of surface water flooding across roads and into surrounding properties. Properties A and B experienced the deepest flooding (water reached thresholds and inundated the ground floor). Residents observed the foul sewer surcharging with lifted manhole covers, indicating surface water entry to the combined sewer. A CCTV survey found blocked gullies (9 and 10) opposite the severely flooded properties.

ref.title: Caterham Drive Flood Investigation Report – 7th June 2016

info.text: Surface water/overland flow from intense rainfall overwhelmed drainage on Caterham Drive. Gullies were found blocked (gullies 9 and 10) and some gullies had suspected collapsed outlet pipes (gullies 4 and 10), reducing drainage capacity. Two properties (A and B) experienced severe internal flooding. A manhole on the carriageway was surcharging and there was physical damage to the carriageway around the manhole cover; video shows runoff from Rydon's Lane onto Caterham Drive. The drainage network was later inspected/cleaned after the event.

ref.title: Section 19 Flood Investigation Report Caterham On the Hill Incident: 7th June 2016

info.text: Surface water flooding and surface-water flow along the Caterham on the Hill piped watercourse / storm route affected the town. Historic highway flooding (wetspots) are recorded in the Caterham on the Hill area and there are recorded instances of internal property flooding in streets within the town; the Money Pit structure on the piped watercourse (adjacent to St Michaels Road) was inspected and being cleaned as part of the response.

ref.title: Section 19 Flood Investigation Report Caterham On the Hill Incident: 7th June 2016

info.text: Surface-water flooding on 7 June 2016 caused property impacts across the town. Local authority response included two Flood Forum surgeries (13 and 28 June) with multiple agencies, a council meeting for residents of Hillcroft Court to assist 18 impacted properties, provision of council tax discounts for displaced households, approximately 70 residents contacting the council for assistance (requests for sandbags, bulky waste collection, council tax enquiries, flood advice) with about 27 follow-ups, an Emergency Parking Order in Park Road to enable contractor parking, additional street cleaning to remove flood debris, and press communications.

ref.title: Section 19 Flood Investigation Report Caterham On the Hill Incident: 7th June 2016

info.text: The catchment in Caterham has a high modelled risk of surface water flooding and contains historic flooding locations. The surface water flow route through the catchment is clearly delineated in model outputs; historic highway flooding (wetspots) and internal property flooding have occurred within the catchment.

info.text: County‑wide impacts from Storm Babet: site visits and flood investigations were undertaken; over 400 structures/assets affected were inspected by Derbyshire County Council; a strategic recovery group was set up and Community Information Officers were deployed by the Environment Agency. Water companies investigated drainage networks, wastewater treatment works, pumping stations and combined sewer overflow facilities.

ref.title: Derbyshire County Council Section 19 Investigation Report – Storm Babet 18/10/23 – 21/10/23

info.text: Between 18 and 21 October 2023 Derbyshire experienced extensive property flooding. Watercourse overtopping was the main cause of property flooding at most communities; surface water flooding was the main cause at some communities and a contributing cause at many; some sewer network flooding occurred where pumping stations were overwhelmed by other sources of flooding. The worst affected communities included Chesterfield, Sandiacre and Long Eaton, with higher concentrations of flooded properties in the Don and Rother, Derwent Lower, and Erewash catchments (east of the county).

ref.title: Derbyshire County Council Section 19 Investigation Report – Storm Babet 18/10/23 – 21/10/23

info.text: Widespread flooding across the county during Storm Babet. A total of 1,647 properties were internally flooded across all eight districts and boroughs. Infrastructure damage recorded included bridge scouring, damage to an electricity substation, and a footbridge washed away. Several roads became impassable causing local traffic disruption. The borough of Chesterfield (within Derbyshire) was especially badly affected, with one resident killed and a large number of properties flooded.

ref.title: Investigation of Flooding Event in Sheffield on 7th and 8th November 2019

info.text: River Don flooded through Rotherham town centre as flows from the upper catchment reached the town; water levels in the Don peaked just after midnight on 7th/8th November. The town-centre river flooding contributed to widespread flooding of businesses and directly caused closure/disruption of rail infrastructure (Rotherham Central station closed due to flooding from the River Don).

ref.title: Section 19 Report November 2019 Floods

info.text: The Don exceeded defence design standards and overtopped in multiple places (notably at Willow Bridge and near Newton Farm), with overtopping at Willow Bridge for approximately 11 hours. Overtopping water travelled north below a railway underpass tunnel then spread north and east filling low-lying land, creating flow routes through residential areas (Riviera Parade, Hunt Lane, Yarborough Terrace, Frank Road) and contributing to filling the Bentley Flood Corridor; overtopping upstream/downstream of Stainforth Bridge also contributed to widespread inundation at Fishlake.

ref.title: Section 19 Flood Investigation

ref.title: Derbyshire County Council Section 19 Investigation Report – Storm Babet 18/10/23 – 21/10/23

info.text: Fluvial flooding from the River Rother and the River Hipper caused internal flooding across central Chesterfield. ref.title: Derbyshire County Council Section 19 Investigation Report – Storm Babet 18/10/23 – 21/10/23

ref.title: Derbyshire County Council Section 19 Investigation Report – Storm Babet 18/10/23 – 21/10/23

ref.title: Derbyshire County Council Section 19 Investigation Report – Storm Babet 18/10/23 – 21/10/23

info.text: The River Hipper overflowed its banks at Queens Park and Ravenside Retail Park, causing internal flooding to businesses in those locations. Floodwater reached approx. 0.7 m depth at a Queens Park business and approx. 0.8 m depth inside an internally flooded business at Ravenside Retail Park; ten businesses at Ravenside/Queens Park were flooded. Hydrology at the Chesterfield Park Road Bridge gauge on the River Hipper recorded an unprecedented peak on 20 October (gauge peak reached 2.93 m). The River Rother overflowed near Hasland Road (about 100 m upstream of its confluence with Spital Brook), causing internal flooding to one commercial property to the west of the river and four residential properties to the east.

ref.title: Derbyshire County Council Section 19 Investigation Report – Storm Babet 18/10/23 – 21/10/23

info.text: The River Rother overflowed its banks at multiple locations in the area, contributing to internal property flooding at Hasland Road, causing flood flows toward the low spot on the A617/Horns Bridge and contributing to flooding of roads, retail parks (including Alma Retail Park) and other infrastructure.

ref.title: Derbyshire County Council Section 19 Investigation Report – Storm Babet 18/10/23 – 21/10/23

info.text: The River Rother overflowed its west bank at Hady Hill and elsewhere, causing internal flooding of the ground floors of The Foundry and Markham Quay apartment blocks, internal flooding of three businesses on Hady Hill between the river and the railway underpass, and internal flooding of properties on Hollis Lane; sewage was reported at some flooded buildings indicating sewer overwhelm.

ref.title: Derbyshire County Council Section 19 Investigation Report – Storm Babet 18/10/23 – 21/10/23

info.text: Floodwater from the River Rother accumulated at a low spot beneath the railway underpass on Hollis Lane / Hady Hill, causing pooling and contributing to internal flooding of nearby properties; individuals evacuated the area by wading through floodwater at depths that exceeded 1 m.

ref.title: Derbyshire County Council Section 19 Investigation Report – Storm Babet 18/10/23 – 21/10/23

info.text: The community sits on the River Rother floodplain and flooding from the river contributed to internal flooding of properties at Meadow Close (New Whittington).

ref.title: Derbyshire County Council Section 19 Investigation Report – Storm Babet 18/10/23 – 21/10/23

info.text: Flooding of the River Rother during Storm Babet affected its floodplain; the river's flood extent reached the area south of Meadow Close and is described as contributing to the internal flooding of nearby homes.

ref.title: Derbyshire County Council Section 19 Investigation Report – Storm Babet 18/10/23 – 21/10/23

info.text: River levels rose from the evening of 19 October, peaking at the Whittington gauge on 20 October 2023 and contributing to the recorded flood extent that affected nearby Meadow Close and Station Lane.

ref.title: Derbyshire County Council Section 19 Investigation Report – Storm Babet 18/10/23 – 21/10/23

info.text: River Rother levels rose sharply (gauge peak 20 Oct) and contributed to the flood extent in the Meadow Close area; floodwater from the river crossed Station Lane and is assessed as likely the dominant source causing the final extent of flooding that led to internal flooding of homes.

info.text: The River Rother may have contributed indirectly by holding high levels that potentially prevented The Moss from discharging, but its direct contribution to the inundation is unclear.

ref.title: Derbyshire County Council Section 19 Investigation Report – Storm Babet 18/10/23 – 21/10/23

info.text: Major incident declared for South Yorkshire on the afternoon of 20th October due to impacts on the River Rother, principally at Catcliffe. Flood warnings were issued for the River Rother at Beighton (123FWF709) and Woodhouse Mill (123FWF711).

ref.title: Investigation Into the Flooding Event In Sheffield On 20th October 2023

info.text: High flows and channel capacity issues on the Rother caused or contributed to flooding in adjacent communities (including near Tapton Terrace and Central Chesterfield); the Environment Agency is assessing whether updated dredging is required and examining flood-defence performance to reduce future risk.
