info.text: Flooding from the main River Aire caused inundation of the lower Aire and its washlands; the event was widespread across multiple authority areas and has prompted an Environment Agency review of flows and washland capacity.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: February 2020

info.text: The River Aire and its associated washlands were involved in the February 2020 flood events; this has prompted the Environment Agency to undertake a review and further assessment of flows and washland capacity (work noted as already in progress since the February 2020 events).

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: February 2020

info.text: Consecutive storms and saturated floodplain caused washlands around Hirst Courtney to reach capacity; River Aire overtopped into the communities of West Bank and Hirst Courtney, and high river levels prevented Black Drain from draining to the river, causing flooding along the Hirst Road corridor between the A19 and Carlton.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: February 2020

info.text: The Lower Aire area was identified as an exception to otherwise isolated incidents and described as a worst-affected area: flooding concentrated along the Hirst Road corridor from the A19 at Chapel Haddlesey to Carlton Bridge in Selby District.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: February 2020

info.text: Fluvial flooding associated with the River Aire affected low-lying land to the south of Chapel Haddlesey and contributed to flood risk/observed flow paths for Chapel Haddlesey and nearby settlements (Hirst Courtney, West Bank, Carlton Chapel Haddlesey). The presence of the weir/old lock influences upstream headwater levels and the flood behaviour at the village.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: February 2020

info.text: The Aire catchment experienced extreme rainfall in February 2020, producing very high river flows and causing river flooding across the catchment during the period.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: February 2020

info.text: Experienced exceptionally high monthly rainfall in February 2020 and intense short‑term rainfall during Storm Ciara and other periods; locations in the Aire catchment recorded 106% to 128% of the February LTA in 48 hours. Persistent rainfall occurred throughout the month and during named storms.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: February 2020

info.text: The Aire catchment (Thornton Moor and Upper Aire locations) experienced persistent rainfall and elevated river flows during February, with sustained runoff particularly around 21 February that increased catchment saturation and contributed to flow peaks.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: February 2020

info.text: Multiple monitoring sites on the Aire recorded significant and, at some sites, record-high peaks during February storm and rainfall events (levels rose during Storm Ciara, rose further during Storm Dennis, and reached monthly/record peaks on 25 Feb).

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: February 2020

info.text: During February the River Aire recorded significant and sustained high flows and water levels driven by successive storms (Ciara, Dennis, Jorge) and saturated catchments. Monitoring sites along the Aire recorded major peaks (including monthly peaks on 25 February) and prolonged elevated levels through the month.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: February 2020

info.text: The River Aire and its catchments experienced widespread flood alerts and flood warnings throughout February 2020 (flood alert for the upper and middle Aire on 8 February; flood warnings for the Aire at Crosshills, Hirst Marsh and West Haddesley on 10 February; warnings for Allerton Ings, Hirst Courtney, Gowdall, Kellington, Hensall, Temple Hirst and repeated alerts for lower/middle/upper Aire catchments across mid- to late-February), indicating significant river flooding risk across the Aire catchment during 01 Feb 2020 - 29 Feb 2020.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: February 2020

info.text: The River Aire flooded its floodplain, inundating agricultural land and encroaching on infrastructure; flooding contributed to failure/damage of floodbank at Temple Hirst (requiring emergency repairs) and impacted transport routes and assets in the vicinity.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: February 2020

info.text: The River Aire was very high following prolonged rain, overtopped into the Lower Aire washlands (washlands exceeded capacity) causing extensive flooding of the Lower Aire Reaches. The Environment Agency deployed pumps to remove water from the washlands back into the river to provide additional capacity.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: February 2020

info.text: The middle and Lower Aire experienced sustained high water levels and successive peaks during the late‑February 2020 rainfall period; washlands did not empty between peaks and tidal/low‑tide elevations within the channel caused rising baseline levels and a noted 'surge' in water levels.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: February 2020

info.text: Floodplain filling of the River Aire over several days raised river levels and contributed to the high levels and flooding observed at Snaith (culminating in high levels on 25 Feb 2020). Flood peaks also passed through Leeds on several February dates.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: February 2020

info.text: Operation of the Leeds Flood Alleviation Scheme (weirs) and the high flows during the February 2020 event increased downstream flows and water levels on the River Aire. The most notable modeled increase was at Thwaite's Mill; downstream water level increases reduced with distance and washlands overtopped at Chapel Haddlesey producing flat-topped gauge peaks.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: February 2020

info.text: Hydrographs across multiple monitoring sites on the River Aire show episodic surges and multiple flood pulses between 9–27 Feb 2020. Those river stage peaks correspond with recorded flooding incidents across communities in western and southern parts of North Yorkshire during February 2020.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: February 2020

info.text: Flood peaks on the River Aire passed through Leeds during the February 2020 heavy rainfall, producing distinct flood peaks in the city.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: February 2020

info.text: The River Aire had flood peaks passing through Leeds and its floodplains filled over several days, contributing to the high levels observed at Snaith; the Leeds FAS weirs on the Aire were operated during the event.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: February 2020

info.text: The River Aire propagated elevated flows downstream during the event; water-level changes at Leeds propagated to downstream gauges (approx. 5 hours to Castleford) and the main flood peak was recorded further downstream at Snaith.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: February 2020

info.text: Further rainfall over Christmas and Boxing Day produced the highest river levels ever seen in many places along the River Aire catchment, contributing to widespread flooding of communities, homes and businesses.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: Record high flows in the River Aire (at Armley) produced very high flood levels that were the main cause of widespread flooding; water also came out of channel approximately 0.8 miles upstream of the Armley flow gauge and flowed down Kirkstall Road towards the city centre.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: The River Aire is identified as a dominant feature and a principal cause of flooding to Leeds and adjacent communities. Its steep profile, rapid response to rainfall and many tributaries contributed to river flooding of Leeds city centre and surrounding areas during Storm Eva.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: Source of deep, fast-flowing flood water that rapidly inundated streets (including Kirkstall Road and Wellington Street) and carried floodwater over a distance into the heart of the city; formal and informal defences were on occasion overtopped or bypassed.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: Flooding originated from the River Aire (a Main River) and is identified in the report as a source of Main River flooding affecting Leeds; the report references flood alleviation measures (River Aire Flood Alleviation Scheme).

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: Identified as one of the District's Main Rivers and a major characteristic of Leeds City Centre; the report states the 25–29 Dec 2015 flooding was almost exclusively a Main River fluvial event, implicating the River Aire as a principal source of fluvial flooding that affected communities along its corridor.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: A Main River fluvial event on 25–29 Dec 2015 along the River Aire caused flooding of areas adjacent to the river and contributed to widespread inundation across Leeds MDC (including multiple Aire-focused sub-areas).

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: Dense clusters of flood incidents occurred along the River Aire through the central Leeds corridor, driving the most severe postcode-sector impacts in central and southern Leeds (City Centre, Kirkstall Bridge/Kirkstall Rd, Hunslet).

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: Historically a major source of fluvial flooding in Leeds (major floods recorded in 1768, 1775, 1790, 1795, 1866 and 1946; further minor instances recorded in 2000, 2002, 2004, 2005, 2007 and 2008). River Aire flooding has threatened the city centre (e.g. images of flooding in Dec 2015) and is a driver for major flood alleviation planning.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: Fluvial flooding from the River Aire inundated parts of the city in December 2015; photographic evidence shows urban streets and infrastructure submerged, impacting the city centre and nearby properties.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: Flow in the River Aire at Armley on 27 December 2015 was the highest ever recorded, producing flood levels approximately 1.2 m higher than the previous record from autumn 2000.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: High flows from the River Aire's source (Malham Cove) following extreme rainfall contributed to downstream flooding; this was a precursor to the Boxing Day floods that affected communities including Leeds.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: Identified in the report as one of the predominant causes of property flooding in Leeds and nearby areas during the event; contributed to the internal and external property flooding counts reported for the metropolitan district.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: Flooding in proximity to the River Aire affected properties across multiple study areas. Reported impacts by area include Leeds City Centre (1938 internal residential; 566 external residential; 296 internal commercial; 55 external commercial), Newlay (5 internal residential; 4 external residential; 1 internal commercial), Kirkstall (0 internal residential; 45 external residential; 36 internal commercial; 15 external commercial), Burley (8 internal residential; 0 external residential; 279 internal commercial; 16 external commercial), Thwaite Gate and Hunslet (60 internal residential; 1051 external residential; 49 internal commercial; 10 external commercial), Stourton (0 internal residential; 0 external residential; 36 internal commercial; 4 external commercial), Woodlesford (1 internal residential; 4 external residential; 0 internal commercial; 1 external commercial), Methley and Mickletown (4 internal residential; 32 external residential), and Allerton Bywater (2 internal residential; 2 external residential; 7 internal commercial).

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: High/record river levels, steep profile and rapid response to rainfall contributed to flooding in Leeds; elevated river levels prevented surface water drainage systems from discharging and caused fluvial backwater effects that led to surcharge of surface water systems and extensive flooding.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: Record-high river levels in the River Aire produced extensive fluvial flooding within flood zone 3, caused fluvial backwater effects that prevented free discharge from the surface water drainage system and led to surcharge/back pressures that produced additional area and surface-water flooding in the city centre.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: The River Aire and its tributaries are shown as the principal loci of flooding, with incidents highly concentrated along the river and largest clusters of flooded properties occurring adjacent to its banks, driving widespread property inundation in central Leeds and riverside neighbourhoods.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: Came out of channel and overtopped its banks at multiple locations in Leeds City Centre (including Little Neville Street, Bridge End/Meadow Lane, Turlow Court, Neptune Street, Clarence Road and Sovereign Street), causing direct flooding of offices, residential properties, assisted living and other commercial areas.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: Overtopping of the River Aire caused flooding of adjacent urban streets and properties (images and captions link overtopping to inundation at Dock Street, Neptune Street, Bridge End and Meadow Lane).

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: The River Aire overtopped its banks (overtopping at Meadow Lane) and raised river levels so high that surface water drainage could not discharge freely for long periods (lasting in some areas for days). These high river levels produced backwater effects and surcharge/back pressures on surface water and sewer systems, which in turn caused flooding of Northern Street, East Street, Sovereign Street, Concordia Street and properties along Whitehall Road as a precursor to later overland fluvial flows. Sewer surcharge related to the high river levels caused roads to become impassable (example: East Street reported impassable after surcharge).

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: High River Aire levels caused sewer surcharge at downstream locations (notably East Street) and contributed to overland fluvial exceedance flows and urban flooding in Leeds, making roads impassable in places.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: The River Aire overtopped upstream in Kirkstall and produced overland fluvial exceedance flows that travelled approximately 2.7 km (over a mile) downstream into Leeds city centre, causing widespread inundation and putting life at risk.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: Rapid runoff and river rise led to the River Aire overtopping its channel capacity, producing widespread fluvial flooding that surcharged surface water drainage and caused backup into gullies, manholes and private drainage.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: The River Aire overflowed its banks at Newlay Bridge, causing river flooding that inundated adjacent buildings, submerged a metal gate, reached lower building windows and partially submerged trees.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: The River Aire was the source of fluvial flooding affecting adjacent Flood Zone 3 areas (incidents clustered close to the river and Newlay Weir), contributing to property flooding in Newlay.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: The River Aire overtopped its banks during Storm Eva (25–29 Dec 2016) in the Newlay area; overtopping and river flow paths sent floodwater into adjacent residential and commercial areas (magenta arrows and overland flow routes on the map). This river-caused flooding produced property flooding in Newlay — Figures 44–47 show residential internal flood damage with verified internal depths of 800 mm to 1100 mm.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: Record/high River Aire levels created fluvial backwater effects that constrained surface water discharge and caused surcharge of surface water systems, which in turn generated extensive surface water flooding in adjacent areas (including contributions to flooding on Savins Mill Way).

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: Extensive fluvial flooding from the River Aire (within flood zone 3) which caused property flooding and disruption in adjacent districts (including Kirkstall and Burley).

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: The River Aire overtopped/caused flooding along its Kirkstall corridor during 25–29 Dec 2015, producing internal and external flooding of built properties (mud and debris evident) and severe internal water ingress in some buildings.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: Overtopped its banks and breached private flood defences in Kirkstall, spilling onto floodplains and directly flooding areas including The Bridge Inn, Leeds rugby academy facility, Morrison's supermarket car park, St Ann's Mills and low-lying properties between the river and Kirkstall Road.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: Experienced extensive fluvial flooding within flood zone 3; record high river levels constrained free discharge from surface water systems, caused fluvial backwater and surcharge that contributed to widespread area and property flooding in adjacent districts (e.g., Burley).

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: Overbank flooding from the River Aire produced the majority of recorded incidents along the river corridor, causing internal flooding to nearby properties (notably in Burley) and area/amenity flooding along the floodplain.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: The River Aire overtopped its banks at multiple locations, breached informal private flood defences and spilled onto adjacent roads (including the A65), producing aggregated flood flows that travelled rapidly downstream into Leeds city centre and caused widespread property flooding and damage.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: Record high river levels caused extensive fluvial flooding within Flood Zone 3. High river levels produced backwater/surcharge effects that rendered surface water drainage (including the nearby pumping station) inoperable until levels fell, contributing to localised flooding; when river levels dropped gravity discharge resumed and local flooding subsided.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: Record high flows in the River Aire led to swollen adjacent waterways and overtopping of channels, producing widespread fluvial flooding and contributing to the inundation of low-lying areas and properties.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: Record high River Aire levels during 25 Dec 2015 - 29 Dec 2015 caused localised flooding influence in low-lying areas of Stourton. Elevated river levels rendered surface-water drainage systems discharging to the river (including the syphon beneath the canal and the nearby pumping station) inoperable until river levels subsided.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: Record high river levels produced fluvial backwater effects that prevented gravity discharge of local surface water systems, contributing to localised flooding in low-lying areas.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: The River Aire produced extensive fluvial flooding within Flood Zone 3 that inundated Stourton and caused property flooding (commercial and external commercial) in the area.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: The River Aire and its watercourses are shown as the primary focus of mapped flood zones and are spatially associated with overbanking/flow routes that led to internal and external property flooding in adjacent Stourton.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: The River Aire overtopped footpaths and contributed overland fluvial flows into the adjacent industrial estate; its interaction with the canal and overtopping routes is mapped as a primary source of inundation.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: Structural collapse of the Knostrop by-wash embankment allowed River Aire waters to enter the canal system, surcharging the Aire and Calder Navigation and contributing to overtopping and downstream flooding.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: River Aire waters breached the by‑wash embankment at Knostrop and inundated the Aire & Calder Navigation canal, contributing to overtopping and flooding of nearby land and properties.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: River Aire overtopped/flowed through the breached Knostrop Lock structure, inundating the adjacent canal and causing significant water flow into the canal system.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: Record high River Aire levels during 25 Dec 2015 - 29 Dec 2015 caused fluvial backwater that rendered surface water drainage systems draining to the river inoperable, produced surcharge/back pressures in surface water systems and led to localised flooding in Woodlesford; standing floodwater inundated industrial units and signage (photograph dated 27 Dec 2015).

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: The river overtopped its channel, spilling onto adjacent floodplains and driving the inundation of the Aire & Calder Navigation; this fluvial overflow was described as the primary cause of flooding that led to low-lying properties and waterside areas being flooded around Woodlesford/Oulton/Swillington.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: The River Aire came out of its channel, overtopping into adjacent floodplains. This overtopping inundated the Aire & Calder Navigation canal and contributed to downstream canal surcharging, breaches and flooding of nearby low-lying properties and land.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: Record-high River Aire levels in late December 2015 caused conventional surface water drainage systems draining toward the river to become inoperable, contributing to localised fluvial flooding in low-lying areas. info.text: Suffered structural damage during severe River Wharfe flooding on 26 December 2015: the south pier settled 200mm overnight and experienced significant scour on its northern side with loose and dislodged foundation stones. The settlement and rotation reduced thrust in the south span toward zero so that a central section (about 5m long, ~150 tonnes) is being held by mortar tension and secondary load paths; failure of the mortar could lead to that section dropping out and a domino collapse of the whole bridge. Monitoring showed movement halted after about a week. Urgent temporary support or controlled demolition and measures to restore and protect the foundation (scour protection) were recommended.

info.text: Town centre and surrounding streets and properties were inundated during the December 2015 events. Photographic evidence from 2015 shows streets, street furniture and property frontages submerged and strong flow across urban streets.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: Extensive fluvial flooding from the River Wharfe within flood zone 3 led to internal and external residential and commercial flooding across Otley. Surface water drainage became inoperable while river levels were high (including issues at the Kell Beck outfall), and fluvial backwater caused surcharge and localised surface water flooding until river levels fell and drainage could discharge by gravity. Streets, low-lying areas and the Wharfe flood plains were affected.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: Fluvial flooding from the River Wharfe overtopped its banks and inundated adjacent floodplains, low-lying properties and amenity areas (including a play area off Farnley Lane almost entirely submerged). Gravel pits to the west filled and fluvial water flowed overland across fields flooding the old cattle market site. The B6451 Farnley Lane at Billams Hill was closed for several hours; homes were completely surrounded by deep, fast-flowing water. Localised surface-water flooding also occurred from Ordinary watercourses where channel capacity was exceeded or culverts were blocked. Otley Bridge acted as a throttle point restricting flows upstream.

ref.title: Leeds Strategic Flood Investigation Report: Storm Eva Flood Event, 25-29 Dec 2015

info.text: Fluvial flooding from the River Wharfe overtopped channel capacity during the 25–29 Dec 2015 event; Otley experienced very rapid river rise (Boxing Day) with the Lower Wharfe reaching its highest recorded levels. Flooding was exacerbated by high river levels surcharging surface water drainage, backing up via gullies and manholes. Otley Bridge acted as a 'throttle point' restricting flows upstream. The town has 300 properties considered at risk of flooding (187 of which were registered to receive Environment Agency flood warnings).

info.text: Across North Yorkshire multiple rivers recorded significant storm-driven peaks during February 2020: River Nidd at Pateley Bridge reached a highest-ever 3.93 m (9 Feb), Bedale Beck at Leeming peaked 4.63 m (9 Feb), River Wiske at Romanby 1.99 m (16 Feb), River Aire sites recorded record or monthly peaks (Roall Dyke 5.95 m; Birkin Westholme 5.4 m; West Bank pond 3.38 m highest on record; Wheelan Dyke 4.59 m highest on record), and Ure and Nidd sites showed pronounced peaks—these measurements reflect widespread river-flood impacts across the county during the storm sequence.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: February 2020

info.text: County-wide flooding during February 2020: nearly every district reported flooding at some level; repeated and prolonged road closures across the month.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: February 2020

info.text: Flooding incidents were recorded across the western and southern parts of the county in February 2020, with isolated incidents linked to Storms Ciara and Denis and to intense rainfall later in the month; localised flood impacts included overwhelmed ordinary watercourses, exceeded beck capacity and overtopping of the River Aire washlands.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: February 2020

info.text: The report refers to February 2020 flooding across the area (including recommendations to monitor Swinney Beck in Masham and for the Environment Agency to review River Aire flows and washlands), indicating the county experienced river flooding during the February 2020 events and that follow-up assessments and resilience works were required.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: February 2020

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report into the flooding in February 2022

ref.title: The East Coast Tidal Surge: 5th December 2013

ref.title: The East Coast Tidal Surge: 5th December 2013

ref.title: The East Coast Tidal Surge: 5th December 2013

info.text: Tidal flooding threat to Boston: concerns about seepage through ground and defences, Flood Alerts issued for the coastline, and contingency planning for possible overtopping or breach of defences. The Environment Agency identified approximately 500 properties at risk from seepage under the forecast scenario and used a worse‑case breach model to identify a further 18,000 properties potentially at risk.

ref.title: The East Coast Tidal Surge: 5th December 2013

info.text: Designated focus for high tide periods; evacuation planning authorised by the Strategic Coordinating Group; flood warnings ('be prepared') issued covering waterside areas including Grand Sluice and the Docks; multi-agency surge task force established to respond at Boston.

ref.title: The East Coast Tidal Surge: 5th December 2013

info.text: Evacuation of known vulnerable people in a predicted flood zone; multi-agency surge task force established; Princess Royal Sports Arena opened as an evacuation processing hub; FRS deployed 6 type B flood rescue boat teams plus support rafts and 7 fire appliances to Boston; Nottinghamshire Underwater Search Unit (13 staff and boat) deployed to Boston; EMAS deployed a HART to Boston.

ref.title: The East Coast Tidal Surge: 5th December 2013

info.text: Higher-than-expected tidal surge prompted EA advice to prepare for possible breaches to defences at the point of high tide; multi-agency evacuation process was fully under-way; FRS received the first call about flooding on Church Street and experienced a dramatic rise in calls lasting about 3 hours; FRS (supported by EMAS HART) carried out rescues and assisted residents isolated by floodwater; the surge task force/bronze relocated operations (Fen Road Depot) due to flood threat to Boston Fire station; evacuees were re-routed and a temporary alternative evacuation centre was used at Stickney.

ref.title: The East Coast Tidal Surge: 5th December 2013

info.text: High tide surge caused water to overtop barriers and flood urban streets and waterside residential properties; water entered business premises on Slippery Gowt Lane; emergency responders (police and FRS) were unable to reach some addresses due to depth and velocity of floodwater; NPAS helicopter deployed to provide overhead visual intelligence.

ref.title: The East Coast Tidal Surge: 5th December 2013

Approximately 220 evacuees transported from Princess Royal Sports Arena to alternative centres; one casualty (asthma attack) recorded. Two IDB high-volume pumps deployed but unable to operate due to insufficient hose lengths/couplings.

ref.title: The East Coast Tidal Surge: 5th December 2013

info.text: Multiple locations within Grimsby experienced internal and external property flooding driven mainly by surcharging sewers (main trunk sewer and highway gullies). ref.title: Merton Section 19 Flood Risk Investigation Report

info.text: Widespread flooding across the borough during extreme rainfall on 12 and 25 July 2021. Sewer capacity was exceeded as large volumes of surface water entered the surface water network; high river levels (Pyl Brook and Beverley Brook) caused backflow, surcharged outfalls and fluvial flooding in some locations. Local factors (topography, gully blockages, sewer configuration) compounded impacts.

ref.title: Merton Section 19 Flood Risk Investigation Report

info.text: The borough experienced multiple surface water / sewer-related flooding hotspots during the July rainfall events, prompting borough-wide recommendations (sewer capacity upgrades, SuDS retrofits, increased gully cleansing and inspection programmes) to reduce recurrence.

ref.title: Merton Section 19 Flood Risk Investigation Report

info.text: Multiple locations within the borough are identified as hotspots and affected locations in the report for the rainfall events of 12 July 2021 and 25 July 2021.

info.text: Morpeth experienced combined river and surface-water flooding on 25/09/2012. info.text: Flooding from Lustrum Beck has led to elevated river levels and overtopping that caused property flooding and localised surface-water flooding. Historical peak levels were recorded (June 2000; November 2000) with November 2000 specifically associated with flooding at Hartburn Avenue. The highest recorded peak was in September 2012 when flooding from a combination of overtopping from the beck and surface water caused reports of properties flooding. During the Storm Eva event (25–26 December) flood warnings were issued for the Lustrum Beck but no properties were reported flooded and temporary defences in the Brown's Bridge area remained dry.

ref.title: Investigation Report Into the Flooding In Cromer In 2016-2017

info.text: Between 1 January 2016 and 31 December 2017 there were 17 reported flooding incidents for Cromer which led to internal flooding of 5 properties (plus 2 further unconfirmed internal reports). Flooding causes reported included overloaded or surcharging drainage systems, drainage/outfall blockages, surface water washed off public highways by vehicles, and surface run-off from roads; flood water entered properties via unprotected building features (low thresholds, unprotected air bricks and service conduits).

info.text: East of Hucknall Road: a combination of surface water and public sewer surcharging caused internal flooding of properties; flood waters entered properties via airbricks, front and back doors and cellars. External depths on Haydn Road rose to between 600 mm and 700 mm and internal flooding in properties was reported between 80 mm and 300 mm; some cellars were flooded to greater depth and one cellar was pumped out. West of Hucknall Road: Haydn Road lies in a valley bottom where steep surrounding roads deliver rapid runoff that can bypass gullies; a former railway bridge underpass near Moores Place forms a ponding low point and properties with thresholds lower than the road have suffered flooding previously. A low-level flood wall with gates was later installed as a response measure.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Daron Gardens & Edern Gardens, Top Valley, Nottingham, On 23rd July 2013

info.text: Overland surface-water flow from the playing fields and along footpaths entered Daron Gardens. Saturated ground prevented infiltration and sheet flow from the steep bank carried silt and debris into gullies. The gully network was overwhelmed and kerbs were breached; water pooled and entered properties via wall vents, airbricks and door frames, moving through houses and exiting via back doors/gardens. A resident reported faeces and black sludge in the flood water, indicating the foul sewer network was also overloaded and contributed to contamination of floodwater.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Daron Gardens & Edern Gardens, Top Valley, Nottingham, On 23rd July 2013

info.text: Overland surface water pooled behind a dividing brick wall at the north end of Daron Gardens. ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Events of November 2019

info.text: Heavy rainfall (notably the torrential downpour on 7 November 2019, with further rain on 9–10 November 2019) caused intense surface water runoff; overwhelmed adopted and private sewerage and highway drainage systems; raised the groundwater table and triggered springs; filled open watercourses so urban drainage could not discharge; and raised main river levels leading to overtopping in some areas. Reports of groundwater emergence and related issues were mainly received from Barton, Barrow, Kirton, Elsham and surrounding low-lying villages.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Events of November 2019

info.text: Heavy rainfall on 7 November 2019 and continued rain caused widespread surface water runoff, overwhelmed sewerage and highway drainage (adopted and private), raised the groundwater table and filled open watercourses so urban drainage could not discharge; main river levels rose leading to overtopping in some areas. The council received reports and followed up with affected residents and RMAs.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Events of November 2019

info.text: The unitary authority coordinated emergency response to the November 2019 floods: a flood incident emergency room was established to organise and coordinate operations; North Lincolnshire Council staff, drainage improvement teams and neighbourhood services provided emergency flooding support; information was issued to the public and recovery activity followed the event.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Benefield Road, Oundle, 24th May 2014

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Warren Bridge, Oundle, 28th October 2013

info.text: Inspection during the flood investigation found a severe narrowing of the watercourse upstream of Stoke Doyle Road with a section of barbed wire across the channel and a build-up of debris, indicating obstruction and elevated flow conditions; downstream reaches were described as narrow and shallow and the brook flows to the River Nene.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Warren Bridge, Oundle, 28th October 2013

info.text: Depth and flow of water from Lyveden Brook caused flooding that affected people and property during the event; listed as the cause of various incidents of flooding on 28/10/2013.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Warren Bridge, Oundle, 28th October 2013

info.text: Banks overtopped; reported to be over one metre higher than normal and flowing strongly. High water from the brook caused high-velocity overland flow across garden boundaries at Warren Bridge, led to significant damage to outbuildings, came close to internally flooding a residential property, and high levels upstream affected sports facilities (closure).

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Warren Bridge, Oundle, 28th October 2013

info.text: An excessive flow in Lyveden Brook caused raised water levels and strong flows that overtopped banks and affected adjoining property; reductions in the cross-sectional area of the watercourse are identified as a factor in the high velocity and depth of flow.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Warren Bridge, Oundle, 28th October 2013

info.text: Reductions to the cross-sectional area of the watercourse and man-made flow controls upstream and downstream of Warren Bridge increased flow velocity and water depth, contributing to flooding at this location; these factors were identified for further investigation by the responsible owners.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Warren Bridge, Oundle, 28th October 2013

info.text: Overtopping / insufficient channel capacity from Lyveden Brook contributed to flooding in the town catchment, prompting recommendations to reinstate historic drainage (re‑excavate ditches, repair/replace piped/culvert sections, dredge and trim watercourses, replace structures and clear vegetation) to reduce future flood risk.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Warren Bridge, Oundle, 28th October 2013

info.text: Lyveden Brook overtopped its banks and discharged muddy floodwater into adjacent private gardens and yards, submerging vegetation and enabling water to reach house bases.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Warren Bridge, Oundle, 28th October 2013

info.text: High water levels observed along Lyveden Brook at the rear of Warren Bridge. Evidence of elevated flows and deposits of debris at a public sewer outfall opposite Warren Bridge.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Warren Bridge, Oundle, 28th October 2013

info.text: High water levels were observed at a public sewer outfall opposite Warren Bridge, with deposits of debris indicating the brook reached elevated levels and overtopped or reached infrastructure margins.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Warren Bridge, Oundle, 28th October 2013

info.text: Lyveden Brook was implicated in the event: ordinary watercourse flooding from the brook contributed to flooding of residential areas near its confluence with the River Nene. Upstream of Stoke Doyle Road a severe narrowing at a large tree, a length of barbed wire across the channel and a build-up of debris were observed, restricting flow and likely exacerbating flooding. Parts of the western developed area drain to public sewers that discharge to the brook, increasing flow into the channel during the event.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Warren Bridge, Oundle, 9th March 2016

info.text: On the morning of 9th March 2016 the depth of water in the brook increased by approximately two metres above usual, causing the banks to be overtopped and water to flow across rear gardens of properties on the north and east edge of the Warren Bridge residential estate. Water levels in gardens and the brook subsided in the late afternoon after the rain stopped.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Warren Bridge, Oundle, 9th March 2016

info.text: Water levels in the brook rose during the event and contributed to higher garden and upstream water depths. Debris (barbed wire) trapped upstream reduced conveyance and caused the channel to become deeper upstream; the narrow, twisting channel downstream limited flow away to the River Nene, contributing to raised water levels.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Warren Bridge, Oundle, 9th March 2016

info.text: Shown with evidence of high water levels; produced overbank and overland flow routes that contributed to schematic flood areas and inundation of nearby rear gardens and properties. Narrowing of the channel and a barbed‑wire obstruction were identified as localised pinch points that increased water levels and localised flooding.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Warren Bridge, Oundle, 9th March 2016

info.text: A barbed-wire fence crossing the brook trapped debris after high flows, creating an obstruction that impeded water flow and contributed to flooding of adjacent banks and nearby gardens/properties.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Warren Bridge, Oundle, 9th March 2016

info.text: Internal flooding of a residential property in the new housing development at the north of the village. The property experienced internal flooding on 14th February 2014 and had been internally flooded on more than one occasion in the previous five years.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Deenethorpe, nr Corby, 14th February 2014

info.text: Surface water from agricultural fields flowed into rear gardens of residential properties in the housing development north of Deenethorpe, flooding a patio and a garage, flowing to the front of properties and a shared private drive, and causing ponding in Deenethorpe Lane. ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Deenethorpe, nr Corby, 14th February 2014

info.text: Surface water from agricultural fields flowed into rear gardens of a housing development north of Deenethorpe. At two properties muddy surface water flowed over property boundaries at significant velocity, reaching approximately 100mm depth on patios. Surface water entered a garage covering the floor and putting an external air-source heating unit at risk. Large deposits of soil were left across a patio area and inside a garage requiring clearance. At a second property surface water and groundwater lifted slab paving at the rear requiring re‑laying. Residents used sandbags to prevent water entering airbricks.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Deenethorpe, nr Corby, 14th February 2014

info.text: Incident Plans (Appendix C) indicate reported routes of surface water across the village during the event.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Deenethorpe, nr Corby, 14th February 2014

info.text: Intense rainfall on a saturated catchment caused existing drainage systems, land drainage ditches and watercourses in Deenethorpe to be unable to cope, causing water to flow into other areas and drainage systems that could not manage the additional quantity of water. Run-off from agricultural land was a significant factor increasing flood volume and risk to vulnerable properties.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Deenethorpe, nr Corby, 14th February 2014

info.text: Surface water runoff from Deenethorpe could not drain effectively to Willow Brook because the brook did not flow or function satisfactorily (see Willow Brook), increasing local flood risk.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Deenethorpe, nr Corby, 14th February 2014

info.text: Properties in Deenethorpe were affected by surface water runoff from neighbouring land and by the emergence of groundwater during the 14th February 2014 event. The report recommends reviewing drainage for the housing development north of Deenethorpe to confirm overland-flow mitigation measures were designed and implemented.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Deenethorpe, nr Corby, 14th February 2014

info.text: Surface water from agricultural fields flowed into rear gardens of residential properties in the housing development north of Deenethorpe, flooding a patio and a garage, flowing to the front of properties and a shared private drive, and causing ponding in Deenethorpe Lane. On 14/02/14 a second property was confirmed affected.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Deenethorpe, nr Corby, 14th February 2014

info.text: Surface water in the village drains to the Main River Willow Brook; the investigation into the 14th February 2014 event recorded internal flooding of one property in the new housing development at the north of Deenethorpe, with runoff discharging to Willow Brook.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Deenethorpe, nr Corby, 14th February 2014

info.text: Very high silt levels at the Deene Park lake inlet and very high water levels in Willow Brook upstream to Osier Bed Lane were observed; these high river levels caused backwater and contributed to standing water on nearby roads and ditches.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Deenethorpe, nr Corby, 14th February 2014

info.text: Runoff and ponded surface water from Deenethorpe Lane drained via road gullies and verge grip drains into Willow Brook, increasing flows in the brook during the event.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Deenethorpe, nr Corby, 14th February 2014

info.text: Willow Brook did not appear to flow or function satisfactorily due to manmade controls forming an artificial lake downstream of the A43, which affected water levels and reduced the brook's ability to receive surface water runoff from Deenethorpe, exacerbating local flooding issues.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Deenethorpe, nr Corby, 14th February 2014

info.text: The brook was impeded by man‑made controls forming an artificial lake downstream of the A43, causing elevated water levels around Osier Bed Lane and reducing the ability for surface water from Deenethorpe to drain into the watercourse.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Deenethorpe, nr Corby, 14th February 2014

info.text: High water level observed immediately upstream of the A43 road bridge and artificial lake, with water close to the base of the bridge arch, indicating limited clearance and risk of overflow.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Deenethorpe, nr Corby, 14th February 2014

info.text: Standing/stagnant water observed in nearby ditches and drainage features adjacent to Willow Brook; verge grips noted between Deenethorpe Lane and Willow Brook opposite the housing development, indicating local overland flow/runoff collecting towards the brook and nearby drainage. These conditions were recorded in association with the investigation of standing water on nearby carriageways.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Deenethorpe, nr Corby, 14th February 2014

info.text: Received discharge from the culvert outlet and the open water course; the channel from the culvert delivered pooled and flowing water into Willow Brook, increasing local flow and conveying sediment/vegetation from the outlet and channel.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Railway Adjacent to Pen Green Lane, Corby, 13 June 2019

info.text: Heavy rainfall increased flows in the watercourse (Willow Brook). Restriction at the flow control culvert/weir caused upstream water levels to rise and water to spill sideways into the balancing ponds; when pond capacity continued to rise flows were routed downstream via the emergency spillway toward Pen Green Lane and the railway aqueduct. The aqueduct and its spillways were at risk of being exceeded, threatening conveyance to the railway drainage at track level.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Railway Adjacent to Pen Green Lane, Corby, 13 June 2019

info.text: The tributary of the Willow Brook at the location of the Corby flood incident was the watercourse involved in the flooding; it is classified as a Main River.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Deenethorpe, nr Corby, 14th February 2014

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Deenethorpe, nr Corby, 14th February 2014

info.text: Ponding occurred in Deenethorpe Lane as water from agricultural fields flowed toward properties; a culvert crossing Deenethorpe Lane to Willow Brook was observed with high water levels, silted pipes and poor maintenance.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Deenethorpe, nr Corby, 14th February 2014

info.text: The village experienced significant rainfall on the Denford catchment leading to high volumes of surface water flowing into lower areas (including Duck End), resulting in internal flooding of at least one property and two properties requiring continuous efforts to prevent internal flooding.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Duck End, Denford, 21st Novermber 2012

info.text: Gardens of residential properties and the highway on High Street were affected by floodwater; an ordinary watercourse culvert beneath High Street was a contributing factor. The River Nene rose to levels that brought properties adjacent to it close to flooding and caused rear gardens to be affected. Large areas of ponding occurred throughout Duck End and Chapel Lane and in the rear gardens of properties on Freeman's Lane because the ordinary watercourse could not discharge quickly enough. At the junction of Duck End and Freeman's Lane a poorly functioning highway gully prevented satisfactory drain down. Large agricultural fields south of Spinney Rise were submerged. Floodwater at Duck End included foul water from the public sewerage system.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Duck End, Denford, 21st Novermber 2012

info.text: Intense, short-duration rainfall on a saturated catchment caused existing drainage systems and watercourses to be unable to cope. Water flowed into areas and drainage systems not designed to manage the additional volume, producing ponding and flooding across Denford.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Duck End, Denford, 21st Novermber 2012

info.text: Intense rainfall on a saturated catchment overwhelmed drainage and watercourses. An ordinary watercourse east of the village was overtopped, producing high-velocity flow into Denford that spanned the full highway width. Existing drainage and culverts (Duck End and High Street) lacked capacity or were in poor repair, preventing conveyance to the River Nene and causing ponding and flooding within the village.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Duck End, Denford, 21st Novermber 2012

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Duck End, Denford, 21st Novermber 2012

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Duck End, Denford, 21st Novermber 2012

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Duck End, Denford, 21st Novermber 2012

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Duck End, Denford, 21st Novermber 2012

info.text: The ordinary watercourse overspilled and produced large areas of ponding through Chapel Lane; the drainage through the rear garden of a property on Chapel Lane collapsed, producing an overland flow to the thresholds of a neighbouring property which would have flooded without continuous efforts by residents and the Fire Service.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Duck End, Denford, 21st Novermber 2012

info.text: Large area of ponding throughout Chapel Lane caused by heavy flow in the ordinary watercourse being unable to flow away quickly enough.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Duck End, Denford, 21st Novermber 2012

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Duck End, Denford, 21st Novermber 2012

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Duck End, Denford, 21st Novermber 2012

info.text: Excess surface water from intense rainfall flowed over ground following natural contours into areas in and around Freeman's Lane.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Duck End, Denford, 21st Novermber 2012

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Duck End, Denford, 21st Novermber 2012

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Duck End, Denford, 21st Novermber 2012

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Duck End, Denford, 21st Novermber 2012

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Duck End, Denford, 21st Novermber 2012

info.text: Areas of flattened grass adjacent to the ordinary watercourse were observed, considered to be evidence of bank overtopping under heavy flows.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Duck End, Denford, 21st Novermber 2012

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Duck End, Denford, 21st Novermber 2012

info.text: Residents on High Street were identified as affected by flooding from main rivers; advice to affected residents was recommended.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Duck End, Denford, 21st Novermber 2012

info.text: Moderate rainfall and ineffective drainage caused excess surface water to flow over ground and along the public highway and around private property; local carriageway/kerb/footway levels directed surface water toward vulnerable properties, resulting in internal flooding of one property.

info.text: Arrangement of kerbs and levels allowed surface water flowing off the carriageway to reach the footway and enter doorways of properties, making areas vulnerable to surface water flooding during the event.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: The Square, Earls Barton, 16th September 2015

info.text: Floodwater overflowed onto the pavement and street area in front of a stone building; sandbags were placed at the building base to protect against ingress; debris and displaced paving material concentrated near the building entrance; construction materials and a traffic cone were affected by the floodwater.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: The Square, Earls Barton, 16th September 2015

info.text: Water entered an internal room at The Square, pooling on tiled floors and affecting furniture and floor coverings. Towels and mats were placed to absorb and contain the water.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: The Square, Earls Barton, 16th September 2015

info.text: Kerb and footway arrangement at The Square with observed gully blockages and leaf accumulation recorded during the flood investigation, indicating reduced drainage capacity and association with surface water flooding at the Square and its junctions.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: The Square, Earls Barton, 16th September 2015

info.text: Kerb and footway arrangement at The Square were photographed during the investigation showing blocked gullies and autumn leaf accumulation at the junction, indicating impaired drainage that would contribute to local surface water flooding and restricted access (temporary barrier visible).

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: The Square, Earls Barton, 16th September 2015

info.text: Surface water sewers flow from High Street to The Square; several road gullies on High Street were observed blocked with leaves and silt during the flood investigation, and runoff from private car parks and hardstanding was seen to flow onto the public highway during the incident.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: The Square, Earls Barton, 16th September 2015

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Main Street, Southwick, 23rd December 2020

info.text: Southwick is traversed by Southwick Brook which has caused historic flooding in the village. Flooding during construction of the Main Street bridge in 1968 and further flooding in the 1990s led to installation of a bypass culvert, bifurcation works and a concrete flood wall upstream of the bridge. When drainage systems are exceeded upstream, overland surface water follows the topography into lower parts of the village and along Main Street; parts of Main Street were previously at a lower elevation and were inundated when the bridge capacity was exceeded. The brook flows to the rear of gardens on Main Street and a nearby ditch and outfall (20m north of Main Street) convey field/woodland flows into the brook; the ditch was noted as largely inaccessible and maintenance was due.

info.text: The village was affected by flooding during Storm Henk (January 2024). The River Trent forms the southern boundary of Gunthorpe and tributaries including the Cocker Beck run through the village; the flooding in the village prompted a Section 19 investigation into which RMAs had relevant functions and responses.

ref.title: Section 19 Report – Gunthorpe – Storm Henk, January 2024

info.text: When the River Trent surges it prevents tributaries from discharging, causing those tributaries to surcharge and other surface-water drainage assets in the village to be unable to function effectively; Gunthorpe is described as having a significant history of flooding and is at high flood risk during the event.

ref.title: Section 19 Report – Gunthorpe – Storm Henk, January 2024

info.text: Village was cut off when the River Trent flooded out of bank; Trent surcharge prevented tributaries discharging so other surface water assets in the village could not function. One property experienced internal flooding from the river; ten properties experienced internal flooding attributed to rising groundwater (residents reported water coming up through floors). Affected areas lie within Flood Zone 3.

ref.title: Section 19 Report – Gunthorpe – Storm Henk, January 2024

info.text: Lowdham village experienced significant flooding produced by a combination of saturated catchment runoff, overland flows and the Cocker Beck overtopping. After the beck began to recede, sewage came up through drains in Blenheim. Drainage was slow down Old Tannery Dyke primarily because a double culvert after Harrison's garage is too high and too small. An Environment Agency-led reservoir scheme upstream is planned to store Cocker Beck flows to reduce future fluvial flooding.

info.text: February storm rainfall and a saturated floodplain caused the Lower Aire washlands to reach and exceed capacity. The Environment Agency deployed pumps to move water from the washlands into the river to provide additional capacity; levels receded over the following days.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Borough-Wide, Sunday 25th July and 7/8th August 2021

info.text: On 25 July 2021 intense torrential rainfall caused widespread flooding across the borough (most affected areas included Walthamstow, Wood Street, Leyton and Leytonstone, focused on the Fillebrook catchment). Water entered homes, schools and businesses, and affected Whipps Cross Hospital; eyewitness reports in worst-hit areas indicated water levels up to 700mm, vehicles were submerged and there was widespread loss of power. Subsequent rainfall on 7 and 8 August 2021 triggered further flooding in these areas.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Borough-Wide, Sunday 25th July and 7/8th August 2021

info.text: On 25 July 2021 intense torrential rainfall caused widespread flooding across the borough (most affected areas included Walthamstow, Wood Street, Leyton and Leytonstone, focused on the Fillebrook catchment). Water entered homes, schools and businesses, and affected Whipps Cross Hospital; eyewitness reports in worst-hit areas indicated water levels up to 700mm, vehicles were submerged and there was widespread loss of power. Subsequent rainfall on 7 and 8 August 2021 triggered further flooding in these areas.

ref.title: Flood Investigation Report: Borough-Wide, Sunday 25th July and 7/8th August 2021

info.text: The borough is subject to both fluvial (river) and pluvial (surface water) flood risk. The River Lea, Ching Brook and Dagenham Brook are identified as the three main rivers/watercourses that are the primary sources of fluvial flooding. The largely culverted Fillebrooke can contribute to localised fluvial flooding at its open channel sections and influences surface water flooding where it forms part of the Thames Water sewer network. Thirteen Critical Drainage Areas (CDAs) have been identified across the borough, with five main CDAs prioritised for drainage management (Group4_064, Group4_067, Group4_054, Group4_048, Group4_047). These CDAs represent corridors and low-lying locations (river valleys, underpasses, railway cuttings/embankments, topographical low points) that are susceptible to deep surface water ponding and sewer-influenced flooding.

Flood levels were observed to recede after the trash screen was cleared. Reported fluvial flooding is attributed to the event on 17 November 2022 and affected properties within Flood Zone 3 adjacent to the recreation ground.

info.text: The culverted watercourse within Westwood Recreation Ground exceeded hydraulic capacity and overtopped its banks, causing flooding of the recreation ground and surrounding properties.
